articles.title: Standard and Digital Mental Health Services on Campus: Perspectives from Students, Clinicians, and Campus Leaders at 27 U.S. Colleges
articles.authors: Naira Topooco, Adam Calderon, Zhaoyi Pan, C Barr Taylor, Ellen Fitzsimmons-Craft, Denise Wilfley, Daniel Eisenberg, Michelle G. Newman
articles.abstract: Objective: This study explored the perspectives of key campus stakeholders on the status of college mental health services and digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) as a strategy to address mental health disorders among college students. Methods: A nationwide online survey (N = 615) was conducted, including clinicians (n = 87) and campus leadership representatives (n = 49) from 27 U.S. colleges and universities during 3 periods of the COVID-19 pandemic (January 2020 to December 2021). Responses from students from a parallel, related sub-study (n = 479) were collated to allow for potential comparisons. The survey assessed the uptake and perspectives of on-campus mental health services and 13 DMHIs. Chi-squared tests and one-way ANOVAs, along with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc pairwise comparisons, were run to tease apart group differences. Linear regression controlling for institutional location was run to examine changes over time on 1) usage of DMHIs, (2) perceptions of implementation interest for DMHIs, and (3) perceptions of delivery feasibility of on-campus mental health services. Results: Leadership representatives, to a higher degree, expressed being ‘Uncertain’ about the presence of training/guidelines than clinicians (75.6% versus 35.5%). Clinicians reported the highest relative degree of use for all DMHIs (M = 6.32, SD = 2.30). Telehealth therapy was viewed among the highest priorities to make available on campus by students (66.0%), clinicians (83.1%), and leadership representatives (82.9%). Students endorsed the lowest perceived delivery feasibility of on-campus mental health services. No significant interactions were found within early to mid to late pandemic periods. Conclusions: Overall stakeholders endorsed marked heterogeneity in uptake and perspectives and were observed not to change over time during the COVID-19 pandemic.

articles.title: Start-up certification and prices: Evidence from markups and a statutory expiry in Italy
articles.authors: Angelo Leogrande, Mauro Di Molfetta, Valeria Nortarnicola, Maria Giovanna Trotta, Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles.abstract: Italy grants registered innovative start-ups fee exemptions, investor tax relief and guaranteed credit, and removes that status sixty months after incorporation. This paper asks whether certification changes firms’ markups. Markups are estimated from a translog production function on 76,466 firm-years of certified start-ups, certified innovative SMEs and ordinary SMEs over 2015–2024. Certified firms price about 12 per cent below ordinary SMEs, but within firms the gap shrinks to 2 per cent and vanishes once persistence is modelled: registration selects firms rather than changing their pricing. Exploiting the statutory expiry, and a 2020 extension that shifted it by one year for adjacent cohorts, the loss of status leaves markups unchanged on average (2SLS −0.005, first-stage F = 750). An unsupervised partition shows this null combines falls of five to six per cent in capital- and materials-intensive firms with none elsewhere; regression learners and double machine learning confirm the central estimates.

articles.title: The Human Cost of Port-Centric Development in Dar es Salaam: Displacement, Congestion and Development Without Distribution
articles.abstract: Dar es Salaam's transformation into a major regional logistics hub illustrates both the developmental promise and distributive risks of infrastructure-led growth. Modernisation of the port, expansion of inland container depots (ICDs), and investment in rail and road connectivity are essential to Tanzania's trade ambitions. Yet infrastructure expansion can generate a second problem when the costs of urban transformation are concentrated on communities living in strategically valuable locations. This article examines the relationship between port-centric development, displacement, compensation and urban congestion in Dar es Salaam, drawing particularly on the experience of Kurasini, the Chamazi community-led resettlement response, recent concerns surrounding ICD expansion, and evidence from the Msimbazi flood-risk project. The analysis argues that the central problem is not simply displacement without compensation but development without distribution. Compensation systems centred principally on recognised property interests can leave tenants and economically dependent residents without adequate assistance to reconstruct their livelihoods. At the same time, the conversion of residential land into logistics infrastructure can create substantial future economic value from which displaced communities have no continuing claim. The article further argues that the proliferation of ICDs within the metropolitan area risks transferring the congestion problem from the port to surrounding communities unless logistics planning is integrated with land-use and rail infrastructure. The appropriate policy response is therefore not to reject port expansion, but to redesign its distributional architecture so that affected populations participate in compensation, resettlement, employment, value creation and the longer-term development dividend.

articles.title: Jumping to Solutions? Bureaucratic Attention Allocation in Response to Negative Performance Feedback
articles.authors: Amandine Lerusse, Joris van der Voet, Wouter Lammers
articles.abstract: Attention allocation is fundamental for governance, policy-making and management in the public administration. The attention-based view highlights how informationally and cognitively constrained bureaucrats allocate their finite attention to diagnose performance shortfalls and identify potential solutions. This study informs bureaucratic attention allocation toward solution-generation and problem-definition using a multi-method approach that combines a laboratory eye-tracking experiment with vignette-based interviews among 41 bureaucrats. We find that bureaucrats process problem-related and solution-related information in sequence and allocate more attention to solution-generation than problem-definition. The interviews demonstrate how the bureaucratic decision context gives rise to role-based, substantive, strategic and aspirational justifications for these patterns in attention allocation. We offer important implications for public administration research, theory and practice, highlighting the ever-increasing demands on bureaucratic decision-makers’ scarce attentional resources.

articles.title: Emotional Intelligence and Money Anxiety: “An Empirical Study on Financial Stress Coping Mechanisms Among Generation Z
articles.authors: Deepika Rathi, Dr Jainish Bhagat, RONAK AJAYKUMAR MEHTA, Komal Sharma
articles.abstract: Generation Z has entered adulthood under a distinctive combination of economic precarity, digital financial exposure, and social-media-amplified comparison, making financial stress a defining feature of their early financial socialisation. While emotional intelligence (EI) is well established in organisational and educational psychology as a predictor of stress regulation, its role in shaping how young adults respond to money-related anxiety remains underexamined in the financial-behaviour literature. This paper develops and specifies a structural model linking Emotional Intelligence, Money (Financial) Anxiety, and Coping Mechanisms among Generation Z, incorporating Financial Self-Efficacy as a boundary condition and Financial Literacy as a control variable. Drawing on the ability model of emotional intelligence (Salovey & Mayer, 1990), the transactional model of stress and coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), and the financial-anxiety literature (Archuleta et al., 2013), seven hypotheses are proposed and a measurement model is specified using established, validated scales — the Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test (Schutte et al., 1998), the Financial Anxiety Scale (Archuleta et al., 2011), and the Brief COPE (Carver, 1997). A Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) approach is proposed as the Page 1 of 23 analytical strategy, given its suitability for exploratory, prediction-oriented models with formative and reflective constructs. The paper details the full measurement instrument, sampling strategy, and a step-by-step PLS-SEM assessment protocol (measurement model validity, structural model evaluation, mediation and moderation testing, and PLS predict) so that the study can proceed directly to data collection and empirical estimation. articles.title: The effects of childhood family disruption on sexual attitudes, experiences and well-being
articles.authors: Yucheng He, Yao Ma, zhuofei lu
articles.abstract: More than 40% of children in the representative UK Millennium Cohort Study experienced a risk of family disruption (i.e., not living with both biological parents by age 14), a circumstance widely recognized as shaping the early developmental environment. Yet the longer-term implications of family disruption for offspring’s sexual attitudes, experiences, and sexual well-being remain surprisingly underexamined. Drawing on 10,624 respondents from the most recent wave (2010–2012) of Natsal-3, and combining weighted OLS and logistic regression models, this study yields several novel findings. First, individuals who experienced family disruption by age 14 face elevated risks of non-volitional sex. Family disruption is also associated with more permissive sexual norms and greater involvement in boundary-testing sexual practices. Moreover, it is linked to slightly poorer sexual functioning and more frequent symptoms of low sexual mood. Taken together, these results provide new evidence that childhood family disruption has enduring consequences for sexual attitudes, experiences, and sexual well-being, underscoring the need for greater attention to interventions supporting children who experience family disruption.

articles.title: Automated Suspicion: Algorithmic Workforce Surveillance and the Erosion of Internal Legitimacy in the Metropolitan Police Service

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Abstract This article examines the Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) pilot deployment of Palantir analytics for internal workforce monitoring, announced in April 2026 as part of the force’s post-Panorama standards programme. The force defends the deployment as lawful, since it brings together data it already holds; this article argues that defence repeats a known mistake in policing legitimacy research, treating legal compliance as the ceiling of consent rather than its floor. Drawing on procedural justice theory (Tyler 2006), the dialogic and twin-track models of legitimacy (Bottoms and Tankebe 2012; Tankebe 2013; Bradford and Tankebe 2014), Beetham’s (1991) account of institutional legitimacy, and the author’s earlier work (Ford 2021, 2026), it audits the deployment against the four pillars of procedural justice and finds it deficient on voice, neutrality, respect, and trustworthy motives. It argues that the pilot inverts Sherman’s (2007) power-few hypothesis, fails the targeting—testing—tracking discipline of evidence-based policing (Sherman 2013), substitutes a technical fix for what Heifetz (1994) calls an adaptive challenge, and entangles culture reform with surveillance in ways that risk delegitimising Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) work and, through a mirroring effect, damaging public-facing encounters. A subsequent disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, including the pilot’s Data Protection Impact Assessment and Equality Impact Assessment obtained in redacted form, tests these claims against primary evidence: it confirms an algorithmic yield of 2.6 million flags with a further-action rate of 0.075 per cent, corroborates self-acknowledged risks to trust and equity in the MPS’s own equalities analysis, and shows the force cannot establish what became of the cases its own system flagged. The article closes with implications for chief officers, police and crime commissioners, and professional standards leads. Keywords: algorithmic management, workforce surveillance, police legitimacy, officer self-legitimacy, procedural justice, psychological safety, organisational culture, EDI, Palantir, Metropolitan Police Service.

articles.title: Towards Developing Indicators of Environmental Sustainability for Kathmandu, Nepal

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Sustainability is now considered one of the key objectives in urban planning. However, due to inappropriate planning, weak institutions, limitation of resources, and poor implementation of policies, many big cities in developing countries have become even less environmentally, economically, and socially sustainable than they were in the past. Historically, the Kathmandu Valley enjoyed a unique tradition, rich heritage and a moderate state of sustainability in all areas, particularly in the environmental arena. However, the rapidly expanding and modernizing cities in the valley are facing serious problems of sustainability on all fronts: economic, social, environmental, and ecological. Whereas, environmental and economic sustainability were tacitly embedded in the traditional planning practices in Nepal, the rapid growth and modernization of the major cities in the valley are making them increasingly unsustainable. This paper proposes major indicators of sustainability and discusses an approach to implement sustainable practices in urban planning and development in Kathmandu.

articles.title: Thoughtforms in the Fog: Liminal Warfare and the Defense of Human Agency
articles.abstract: Cognitive warfare is commonly framed as a contest over perception and decision-making. This article argues that its most consequential leverage often appears during liminal periods, when established identities, meanings, and institutions no longer provide sufficient orientation. It introduces the thoughtform as a functional analytic construct with a long, heterogeneous genealogy in initiation, ritual, and esoteric reflection, but does not rely on metaphysical claims. A thoughtform is defined here as a recursively sustained symbolic formation that organizes attention, emotion, identity, interpretation, and action across people, media, institutions, and machines. A six-stage Liminal Thoughtform Cycle explains how threshold disruption can produce either adaptive integration or cognitive capture. The article then advances liminal security and Cognitive Aikido as agency-centered defenses, treating mental health and well- being as capacities for sustaining meaning, relationships, reality orientation, and action under pressure. The objective is capacity rather than control: preserving reflective freedom, relational coherence, and meaningful action under persistent influence. Keywords: cognitive security, cognitive warfare, liminality, thoughtforms, influence operations, agency, resilience

articles.title: Co-creating change in agriculture and food systems: A systematic review of co-creation processes and approaches for evaluating their contributions to sustainability transformation
articles.authors: Sara Delaney, Sophia Alami, Maria Busse, Bonnie Averbuch, Fanny Boeraeve, Pauline Cassart, Valéria Csonka, Graeme Dean, Cedric Gossart, Bienvenu Kambashi
articles.abstract: Co-creation is widely proposed to address complex sustainability challenges by bringing together diverse forms of experience and expertise. Yet practical, evidence-based guidance on how co-creation processes can support sustainability transformation remains fragmented and insufficient, including for agriculture and food systems. We conducted a systematic literature review to characterize scholarly work on co-creation for environmental sustainability and to identify process insights relevant to Living Labs and related participatory initiatives. Following a four-stage screening procedure, we reviewed 5,291 articles and retained 266 studies describing multi-stakeholder, action-oriented, experimental processes; 51 agriculture- and food-focused articles were subjected to in-depth qualitative analysis. We combined bibliometric and descriptive analyses, including co-authorship network mapping, with framework-guided qualitative coding of co-creation inputs, processes, outcomes, impacts, and evaluation practices. Publications on this topic increased substantially over the past decade, but relatively few studies documented action and experimentation in sufficient methodological detail. Agriculture and food studies constituted a moderately self-contained segment of the broader literature. Across the qualitative sample, five enabling factors were most consistently associated with productive co-creation: participant alignment, institutional support, strong facilitation, inclusive participation and trust, and sufficient time for iteration. Studies also identified recurring trade-offs between diversity and alignment, resource-intensive engagement and scalability, and place specificity and transferability. Frequently reported outcomes were new knowledge, communication and networks, empowerment or efficacy, and skills. However, evidence of longer-term sustainability impacts was limited: most articles described intermediate outcomes rather than demonstrated transformation. Only sixteen articles evaluated the co-creation process itself, and participatory development of evaluation criteria was rare. Co-creation efforts can build the practical and relational capacities, and “social infrastructure” needed for sustainability transitions, but stronger methodological reporting and participatory, longitudinal evaluation are needed for validation of criteria and proxies for impact and establishment of how these processes contribute to lasting transformation.

articles.title: Negotiating mobility: Methodological insights from older adults' activity diaries
articles.abstract: Older adults' mobility is a growing area of research, with multiple methods being employed to understand whether older adults can adequately access key destinations. This has resulted in increased interest in older adults' activity spaces, and a concomitant rise in methods employed to work with these individuals. While GPS-based data collection has advantages, traditional paper surveys remain in use due to their perceived low barriers to entry for participants and researchers. Relatively little is known regarding the appropriateness and validity of paper-based, self-reported activity diary data collection with older adults. Using qualitative feedback on activity diary surveys deployed in rural and urban communities and the activity diaries themselves, we argue that paper, self-reported activity diaries are viable instruments for recording older adults’ geographies. Further, qualitative feedback demonstrates how older adults confront their mobility, memories, and communities. We identify perceived mobility deficits, difficulties remembering, community visibility, and positive affect among our participants. Our findings suggest participating in activity diary surveys is a generally positive experience for older adults, but for some may engender a sense of inadequacy regardless of their activity level. We make recommendations for methodological enhancements specific to working with older adults.

articles.title: The Illusion of Precision: Interpreting International Rankings Within Their Measurement Limits

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: International rankings publish precise country positions. We ask which comparisons the evidence behind five of them supports, by reproducing published tables, optimising weights, applying multiplicity-adjusted rank inference and two source checks, within a framework separating invalid measurement, insufficient validation, normative trade-offs, underrepresentation of uncertainty and misleading communication. In every programme the adjacent ordering is unsupported, each for a different reason: Report Card 19 trades off dimensions in all 35 adjacent pairs; World Happiness Report countries move a median of 30 places when affect replaces life evaluation; 23 of 38 countries can lead the Better Life Index under unrestricted weights; retrospective rescoring moves Global Health Security Index countries a median of seven places within one year; only 4 of 80 adjacent PISA pairs are distinguishable. Broad contrasts survive throughout. Two unrepresented uncertainties are documented: rotated administration behind Report Card 19's social-skills indicator, and unlinked assessment vintages behind the Human Capital Index.

articles.title: Structured Literature Analysis on Sustainability Report Disclosure in Public Sector Organizations
articles.authors: Muhammad Arifai, Mariana Mariana, Heru Fahlevi, Mirna Indriani, Darwanis Darwanis
articles.abstract: Objectives: This study examines the adoption of sustainability reporting in Public Sector Organizations (PSOs), focusing on (1) stakeholder expectations, (2) implementation challenges, and (3) the impact on accountability and value creation. It also identifies existing gaps in sustainability reporting frameworks and provides strategic recommendations to enhance transparency and effectiveness in public sector sustainability disclosures. Methodology: A Structured Literature Review (SLR) was conducted on 97 articles from Scopus (1990–2024), selected using keywords such as "sustainability reporting," "public sector," "GRI framework," and "public sector organizations." Inclusion criteria ensured relevance to the public sector and methodological diversity. The articles were categorized by sustainability focus, country, research methods, and theoretical frameworks. This approach enabled the identification of research trends, key gaps, and best practices to support policy improvements in sustainability reporting. Findings: The review reveals that (1) research on sustainability reporting in PSOs is still limited and predominantly conducted in developed countries, (2) there is an increasing trend in sustainability reporting driven by demands for greater transparency and accountability, (3) major challenges include inconsistencies in reporting frameworks, varied stakeholder expectations, and difficulties integrating sustainability metrics, and (4) adoption is influenced by regulatory environments, political commitment, and resource availability. Although digital reporting tools are emerging, standardization and performance measurement issues remain unresolved. Conclusion: Despite progress, sustainability reporting in PSOs suffers from a lack of consistency, comparability, and stakeholder engagement. To improve credibility and effectiveness, harmonized standards, stronger regulatory oversight, and capacity-building initiatives are essential. Addressing these gaps will enhance accountability and foster long-term value creation in the public sector.

articles.title: The Kia-Hyundai vehicle theft surge: the roles of anti-theft devices and co-occurring offenses
articles.abstract: Between 2020 and 2024, vehicle theft in the United States increased 40 percent. This study addresses this as a natural experiment, using a quasi-experimental design for causal inference to attribute the increase to theft of Kia and Hyundai vehicles manufactured without engine immobilizers. It is conservatively estimated that by the end of 2024 there were over 1.1 million excess vehicle thefts and over three hundred thousand excess co-occurring offenses including homicides, violence and other serious offenses. The evidence indicates that the withdrawal of situational crime prevention measures can increase crime and criminality and that the long-term national crime declines cannot be taken for granted. Additional implications are identified.

articles.title: The weaponised Ocean and marine spatial planning
articles.abstract: Restrictive asylum and border policies force people into dangerous maritime crossings and lead to record numbers of deaths at sea. Yet marine spatial planning (MSP), despite commitments to social benefit and expanding attention to diverse marine uses and stakeholders, has largely overlooked irregular migration and the governance regimes that shape these routes and their lethality. Applying border geographies literature to European seas, we highlight the Ocean as a weapon used to control migration and allow states to shift responsibility onto migrants. In this Short Communication, we argue that the weaponisation of the sea through deterrence, pushbacks, neglect, and externalised border control should be recognised as an issue of marine governance. While MSP has limited scope to resolve structural drivers of displacement or border violence, it can no longer remain silent on spatially patterned forms of ‘liquid violence’. Analysing irregular migration through MSP could support more just and humanitarian Ocean governance through improved spatial understanding of migration routes, risks, and sites of death, and by aligning planning more explicitly with the protection of human life at sea. We argue that irregular maritime migration and death at sea should be understood as concerns for marine governance because they are spatially patterned, politically produced, and shaped by the allocation of visibility, safety, and responsibility at sea. As migration drivers continue to increase, acknowledging and addressing these neglected realities is an urgent task for marine policy and planning.

articles.title: Mezi kontinuitou a změnou: Městské názvosloví a postsocialistická transformace v perspektivě kritické toponymie / Between Continuity and Change. Urban Toponymy and Post-Socialist Transformation from the Perspective of Critical Toponymy
articles.abstract: The naming of public spaces is a popular tool that ruling regimes have used since the second half of the 19th century to imprint their values on the public sphere and to express symbolic power. However, due to frequent changes in the political and social context, urban naming systems also change frequently. The most recent significant intervention in Central and Eastern Europe was the collapse of the Eastern Bloc in the early 1990s. Among the main features of the wave of post-socialist renaming were a widespread “cleansing of sins”—that is, the restoration of original names to places that had been renamed during the communist dictatorship—as well as numerous disputes and dilemmas regarding which names to remove and what to replace them with. Naming policy stems from a broader political and historical context, but ultimately it is always the result of negotiations within specific local conditions. This paper examines changes in city names—known as urbanonymy—through the lens of critical toponymy, which links cultural and political geography with history, memory studies, or anthropology. It presents the main trends in the transformation of urbanonymy in the period following the collapse of the socialist bloc and, based on selected works, offers insight into specific situations involving the renaming of public spaces, with a particular focus on Czech and Slovak cities. At the same time, it highlights a renewed wave of interest in lingering socialist toponyms and their repoliticization in the context of Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine after 2014.

articles.title: Maximizing Recruitment via Respondent-driven Sampling
articles.authors: Mariel Leonard, Julian B. Axenfeld, Hannah Bethge, Julia Witton, Carina Cornesse, Sabine Zinn
articles.abstract: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS), a network-based method of sampling has become increasingly popular as a means of developing subgroup samples, particularly in web-first or web-only design (webRDS). WebRDS can reduce participant burden as well as increase the potential size and geographic scope of the sample, allowing for development of national samples with greater generalizability. However, webRDS can also introduce technical challenges as it requires all RDS processes to be mediated through internet-communication technology. In this paper, we focus on the challenges of engaging participants and reducing burden following a request to participate in webRDS. We present the results of two studies in which we tested several design features for their effects on webRDS recruitment success. We use social exchange theory as a lens through which to improve webRDS recruitment by maximizing benefits of participation and reducing burden. Based on our findings, we present recommendations for webRDS implementation.

articles.title: Digital media and social inequality : a primer in the context of Swiss digital society
articles.abstract: Digital media innovations are used differently by people from different social groups and have varying consequences. Research has not found that these divides are narrowing. On the contrary, individuals who are socially better positioned appear to benefit more from digital media transformation. At the societal level, there is a need for a transparent negotiation of the values underlying the digital media infrastructure - values that can guide democratic governance.

articles.title: ‘My spiritual path is Belonging’: Belonging as a valued and sought after affective state for spiritual but not religious individuals.
articles.authors: Kathryn D. Ford, Sotirios Kolios, Lora Adair, Matthew M. Gervais, Aiyana Willard, Michelle Kline
articles.abstract: Abstract Objective: Spiritual but not religious (SBNR) beliefs are often characterised as hyper individualistic and lacking community. This study explores concepts of belonging and community among spiritual seekers to assess these claims. Methods: This study entailed 30 semi-structured interviews of SBNR individuals combined with long term ethnographic research in Glastonbury UK, a small town with a reputation as a spiritual hub. Results: Thematic analysis of participant interviews highlighted the importance of affective belonging to participants. Participants left social contexts where they experienced a lack of affective belonging. Participants invested time and effort into finding sources of affective belonging and in creating sources of affective belonging for others. Conclusion: Affective belonging is important to SBNR individuals. Prior research suggesting that spiritual but not religious do not value belonging is due primarily to miss-measurement and a lack of conceptual clarity. Key words: Spiritual but not Religious, Belonging, Community, Glastonbury, Belief, Qualitative, Interviews

articles.title: Capacity development approaches and strategies in climate change adaptation projects in Latin America: A typology
articles.authors: Caroline Nye, Paul Cisneros, Sarah-Lan Mathez-Stiefel, Manuel Fischer
articles.abstract: The success of climate adaptation projects globally is dependent upon a multitude of factors, including the various actions which are designed into a project, as well as more contextual factors affecting the delivery of those actions. Capacity development, sometimes referred to as capacity building, is one type of action which has been identified as having the potential to improve the delivery of a project but perhaps, more importantly, ensure its impact and sustainability beyond the limitations of a project. Using mainland Latin America as a focus region, this paper analyses 60 ‘real world’ climate adaptation project proposals, funded by three different multilateral climate finance mechanisms, in order to highlight the principal characteristics of the capacity development strategies across all projects. Through the manual coding of each proposal, a typology of twelve different ‘types’ of capacity development actions was created, which seeks to outline the specific delivery modality and strategic approach employed by a project, taking into account learning dynamics and possible power relationships. In addition to the typology as an output, findings demonstrate that consideration of capacity development elements remains insufficient across many projects, and that, while there has been movement towards strategies emphasising empowerment, local ownership and long-term change, a significant shift is still required: one which moves away from a reliance upon traditional top-down methods of developing knowledge and coordinating stakeholders, to initiatives which include more participatory, iterative and enabling actions.

articles.title: Geometry Proposes, Judgement Disposes: Accurate Online Proposal Clustering for Digital Deliberation
articles.abstract: Digital deliberation requires accurate clustering of proposals: equivalent contributions should be joined, while related interventions and opposing positions remain distinct. We study an online method implemented in Freedi that uses embeddings to retrieve candidates and focused language-model judgements to authorize synthesis, with separate themes, retained sources, and maintenance. We explain its retrieval-judgement interface and seven-stage selection process and compare it with the two main alternatives, cosine rules and LLM-only grouping. On 875 counterfactual preference triplets, a component study achieves 95.0%-96.5% accept-and-reject accuracy with original-text judging, compared with 0% for the tested cosine decision rule. On a controlled English corpus, Freedi and LLM-only baselines recover all 50 intended pairs in three arrival orders. A new 240-call probe on one authentic English deliberation compares full-list judgement with judgement over 15 retrieved proposals. Median per-decision cost reductions grow from 2.55-fold at 100 proposals to 4.29-fold at 200 and 9.38-fold at 500, under common base token prices. At 500 proposals, agreement with provisional model-authored labels is 25/40 for the restricted list and 31/40 for the full list. Retrieved targets remain available, but the restricted judge declines more merges. These refusals may preserve substantive distinctions in scope or intervention; whether they improve semantic precision or constitute missed matches requires human adjudication. A separate replay of 114 Hebrew statements shows improved automated merge precision and text fidelity after combined repairs. The evidence supports semantic judgement over the tested cosine rules and a growing cost advantage for candidate reduction at the measured scales. Equal accuracy and lower total cost for the complete Freedi pipeline remain to be established.

articles.title: Perspectives on integrating robotic, bionic, and bioprinting technologies in healthcare
articles.authors: Alyna T. Khan, Audrey Nankervis, Carson Knight, Sara Gerke, Jennifer K. Wagner
articles.abstract: Purpose: Advancements in robotic, bionic, and bioprinting technologies have potential to transform healthcare. Their rapid development and swift adoption in clinical and commercial domains are outpacing ethical, legal, and policy frameworks. Thus, examining how to incorporate these emerging technologies responsibly and effectively into our societal context is an urgent concern. In this study, we investigate the perspectives of subject-matter experts with experience in robotics, bionics, and bioprinting to better understand their needs and concerns regarding the integration of these technologies in healthcare. Methods: We conducted a qualitative interview study with legal experts (attorneys or law scholars) and scientists/technologists (N=31) using a semi-structured interview guide covering topics on a variety of ethical, legal, and social matters (ELSI) involving data justice, regulation, and public acceptance of technologies. Results: Participants expressed uncertainties about the regulatory approval process and need for new frameworks to address emerging technologies. Participants also highlighted key systemic factors in the current US healthcare infrastructure that need to be reconsidered to effectively operationalize robotic, bionic, and bioprinting technologies in healthcare. Discussion: Interdisciplinary dialogue and incorporation of ELSI perspectives are needed to address such concerns. Future research should further examine specific ethical, legal, and policy needs to responsibly integrate advanced technologies in healthcare.

articles.title: Digital health equity in bionic devices: A systematic review
articles.authors: Alyna T. Khan, Julia M. Kline, Sara Gerke, Jennifer K. Wagner
articles.abstract: Background: Bionic devices use digital technology to restore, improve, and/or monitor physical abilities and natural functions of the body. As high-tech solutions to healthcare become increasingly available, consideration for digital health equity is urgently needed. Applying the Digital Determinants of Health (DDoH) framework, this review explores how equity considerations are integrated in the research literature of bionic devices in healthcare. Methods: Using PubMed, we conducted a limited systematic literature review of bionic devices that address a variety of human healthcare needs. Of the 201 nonduplicate, peer-reviewed records screened, we summarize findings from 100 eligible research articles describing the scientific literature’s coverage of digital health equity concerns in bionic device research and implementation. Results: We found 48 articles that explicitly addressed one or more aspects of the DDoH framework and 30 articles that offered no explicit consideration of the digital health equity framework. Of the studies that focused on digital bionic devices (N=78), 27 mentioned individual-level influences of health, while 19 mentioned interpersonal-level influences of health. Societal-level influences were discussed in 23 articles, while community-level influences were each discussed in 13 articles. Conclusion: Successful uptake of bionic devices requires a nuanced understanding of individual, interpersonal, community, and societal needs. While studies mention individual- and societal-level concerns for equity, we observed a gap in the discussion of interpersonal- and several community-level influences. Research examining the data practices, data privacy, and dataveillance risks (among other ELSI dimensions) of bionic devices can inform policy in ways that encourage equitable development and data use practices and ensure bionic device technologies benefit everyone. Researchers and developers should incorporate digital health equity considerations into bionic device development and applications for responsible integration and equitable use.

articles.title: Digital Public Infrastructure’s Promise of Financial Inclusion and the Reality of Digital Lending: A Comparative Approach
articles.abstract: In the past decade, digital lending has become central to a new developmental imaginary in India. The introduction of the Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) approach in India has been narrativized as a revolutionary feat, drawing praise from international institutions and private sector alike. The rollout of these state-promoted platforms for identification, payments, and data sharing is said to be creating new possibilities for micro-entrepreneurship and market participation, lifting the poor out of poverty. Yet in reality, digital lending’s reach among women is limited, and instead its main market is among men. In this article, we ask: why, despite the developmental claims and ambitions of DPI, does the reality of digital lending in India remain limited in reaching women? The paper compares digital lending with two earlier “financial inclusion assemblages”, public banking and microfinance to identify how each organizes credit, whom it reaches, and what kinds of social futures it imagines. It finds that the limited reach of digital lending among women reflects not a limitation of digitalisation itself, but rather a mismatch between the architecture of DPI-enabled digital lending and the needs of women and other marginalized communities. Addressing these failures, the paper concludes, requires a significant realignment of the role of DPI in relation to digital lending. Problems of reach and access are reframed as issues of structure and conditions of access.

articles.title: Does Reading a Compassionate Story Improve Children’s Helping in the Compassionate Responding Paradigm?
articles.authors: Frankie T. K. Fong, Kelly Kirkland, Prerna Nagesh, James Kirby
articles.abstract: Recent findings using the compassionate responding paradigm suggest that preschool children will not help a distressed target (puppets or adults) when it is costly to do so. This registered report examined whether reading a storybook that promotes compassionate behavior translated to greater costly compassionate helping using the same experimental paradigm. The first part of our study involved parents reading either a book promoting compassionate action or a control book with their children across a 1-week period. The storybook was sent to parents, along with reading guidelines and a short reading diary (which parents filled in every day). Children were then invited to participate in the compassionate responding paradigm. We expected a higher level of compassionate helping for children who read the compassionate storybook compared to children who participated in the control condition, however our results did not support this hypothesis. This study affords important insights into whether preschool children are responsive to stories that promote compassionate action. It also raises discussions about the scope and limit of the compassionate responding paradigm.

articles.title: Constructing Methodologically Robust Subnational Estimates from Survey Microdata: A Methods Review
articles.abstract: Constructing estimates for a custom, county-defined region from survey microdata is constrained by the geography at which respondents are identified. In the American Community Survey (ACS) Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS), that geography is the Public Use Microdata Area (PUMA), which does not nest into counties and is periodically redrawn. This review surveys the state of the art in producing methodologically robust subnational estimates under these constraints, organized into four method families — crosswalk and allocation-factor methods, consistent-geography harmonization, areal interpolation and dasymetric and structure-preserving methods, and model-based small-area estimation. Each family is assessed against a reference baseline: a population-weighted allocation-factor pipeline with Successive Difference Replication variance estimation. The review pays particular attention to the within-zone compositional homogeneity assumption that limits direct reweighting, to the harmonization of geographies across boundary revisions, and to the rigor of uncertainty quantification. It restricts attention to methods implementable with publicly available data. It serves both as a standalone reference and as the methodological foundation for a companion analysis.

articles.title: Questionnaire Design and Rater Cognition in 360-Degree Performance Appraisal
articles.authors: Saber Mirzaei Ahandani, Simin Ebrahimi Lialekol
articles.abstract: Questionnaire design may play an important yet underexamined role in shaping the quality of performance appraisal data. This study examines whether redesigning response formats in a 360-degree feedback system is associated with improvements in rating behavior, response quality, and psychometric consistency. Drawing on cognitive processing and response-process perspectives, we compare a traditional numeric Likert-format questionnaire with a redesigned format incorporating behaviorally descriptive response options, modified visual presentation, and variable response ordering. Data were collected across two appraisal periods within a large production organization employing more than 25,000 individuals. A total of 26,672 questionnaires were distributed, and 18,621 responses were obtained for the evaluation of approximately 900 managers in different levels. Following the redesign, participation rates increased from 47% to 79%, and internal consistency reliability improved from Cronbach’s α = 0.902 to α = 0.939. Response distributions also became less concentrated in extreme categories and more evenly distributed across intermediate categories, indicating greater rating differentiation and reduced response bias. These findings are consistent with the argument that behaviorally descriptive response formats encourage greater cognitive engagement and reduce reliance on heuristic responding during performance evaluation. The study contributes to performance appraisal and multisource feedback research by highlighting the role of questionnaire design in shaping response processes, rating behavior, and measurement quality. Together, the findings provide evidence compatible with the view that relatively small and scalable questionnaire design modifications may enhance cognitive engagement, improve measurement quality, and increase the validity and practical usefulness of organizational appraisal data.

articles.title: Economic Growth and Working-Class Representation: Evidence from Brazil
articles.abstract: Economic growth may lead to more resources for the working class to solve collective action problems and demand political representation, but not all instances of economic growth do unequivocally reduce economic inequality. When productivity gains accrue disproportionately to economic elites and political parties lack durable ties to labor, it may instead deepen class-based political exclusion. I test this argument using a novel panel that identifies the occupational background of every city council candidate in Brazil from 2004 to 2020, a period of economic growth led by agribusiness productivity increases. Within municipalities, increases in GDP are associated with a smaller share of campaign funding going to working-class candidates and a lower share of elected councilors from working-class backgrounds. Leveraging individual-level data on career trajectories of incumbents, I confirm these results. Additionally, I study the scope conditions for my theory, showing that non-leftist parties and rural areas drive my results. A qualitative comparison design reveals that discretionary choices by party leaders serve as a channel through which unequal growth can reinforce exclusion in political representation.

articles.title: Are geographical and socioeconomic contexts exchangeable? On simple means versus random effects in the study of health inequalities
articles.abstract: Multilevel random-effects (RE) models are standard in social and geographical epidemiology. They rest on the assumption of exchangeability, which means that, before seeing the data, we have no reason to distinguish one group from another: group means become draws from one common distribution. RE models were developed for repeated measurements within individuals where a shared physiology underwrites the assumption, and partial pooling improves prediction. A silent transfer later applied the same machinery to schools, hospitals, neighbourhoods and, recently, to intersectional strata. There exchangeability fails twice: individuals are not repeated measurements of their group, and groups are social positions produced by directional forces such as racism, not draws from a common distribution. We review strict, conditional and tolerant readings of exchangeability and show that they agree: social and intersectional categories are not exchangeable, as this would paradoxically require the absence of the unjustified inequalities which are the very object of study. In many intersectional analyses, shrinkage erases the small and deviating strata, where inequality lives. Modelling injustice as dispersion around a mean domesticates rather than denounces it. For describing realised health inequalities we recommend Simple-Means MAIHDA (S-MAIHDA). Here, each stratum is estimated from its own individuals, and uncertainty is reported openly rather than smoothed. RE models keep their legitimate uses, such as prediction, cluster-randomised trials and the propensity models of causal S-MAIHDA. Exchangeability is not a property of the software. It is a claim about the world, to be justified in every application.

articles.title: Six-Year Trends in LGBTQ+ Youth Mental Health in the United States
articles.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of trends in LGBTQ+ youth mental health from 2019 through 2024, drawing on data from The Trevor Project’s annual national surveys. We examine five consistently measured indicators across six years of survey data including: suicidal ideation and attempts, discrimination due to SOGI (sexual orientation and gender identity), physical threats and harm exposure, and conversion therapy exposure and threats. Suicidal thoughts among LGBTQ+ youth rose to a significant peak before easing, while actual attempts showed a steady decline, especially among adolescents, yet younger teens remained disproportionately vulnerable throughout. Over the same period, discrimination remained persistently widespread, while reports of physical violence swung sharply but ended higher than at the outset, and exposure to conversion therapy spiked briefly during the pandemic era before settling back to its earlier yet still troubling level, highlighting the significant risks young LGBTQ+ youth and young adults face. The findings highlight continuing disparities, alongside small improvements in some areas. In conclusion, we summarize key insights and recommend actions to bolster mental health support, reduce stigma and victimization, and expand affirming resources for LGBTQ+ youth.

articles.title: The Latent Interview Protocol: Recovering Enacted Question Structure for Large-Scale Interview Analysis
articles.abstract: Interview researchers increasingly work with large corpora for which traditional line-by-line coding is costly. Current proposed indexing strategies to make the corpus more manageable still require line-by-line indexing while assuming that the planned interview protocol accurately represents what was asked in practice. This article introduces the latent interview protocol—the recurring substantive questions that organize interviews as enacted, along with the pathways linking them—and LIPE, an open-source workflow that recovers this structure by combining sentence embeddings, density-based clustering, and researcher-guided refinement. Validated protocol questions are assembled into a corpus-level structure and used to retrieve local response blocks for downstream qualitative analysis. An application to 63 semi-structured interviews on mothering during COVID-19 shows that LIPE recovers most planned protocol questions, surfaces emergent lines of inquiry, and retrieves question-anchored responses with high precision and recall. The approach makes large-scale interview indexing more tractable while preserving interpretive control over analytic boundaries.

articles.title: Accessibility as Infrastructure: A Neurodivergent Led Model for Structural Communication Safety in Disability Support Systems

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Disabled people frequently experience communication collapse during distress, overwhelm or coercive control, producing indirect, fragmented, masked or delayed expression rather than clear verbal articulation. National Inquiries – including the Disability Royal Commission (2023) and the NDIS Review (2023) – demonstrate that current disability and safeguarding systems are misaligned with these communication realities, relying on speech, privacy, cognitive stability and narrative coherence at precisely the moments that these capacities fail. Communication Collapse is there a predictable, embodied response shaped by trauma, cognitive load and social misunderstanding, rather than and individual deficit. This article introduces accessibility as infrastructure, a conceptual reframing that positions communication safety as a structural requirement of safeguarding systems. Drawing on disability studies and critical social theory, it argues that safeguarding infrastructures must be redesigned to recognise neurodivergent communication as valid and actionable, particularly during shutdown, overwhelm, masking, executive- function collapse and coercive control. Within this framework, the article presents Althing, a neurodivergent-led, trauma informed safeguarding model engineered to remain usable during distress-state communication collapse. By supporting early, low-detail, indirect or delayed signals of harm, Althing addresses structural communication failures and aligns with national reform expectations for trauma-informed, low-demand safeguarding pathways. Although conceptual, the model offers a mature foundation, for future co-design, empirical evaluation, and state-level safeguarding innovation, demonstrating how accessibility as infrastructure can strengthen communication safety at the exact moments disabled people are least able to seek help.

articles.title: A Rough Revised Estimate of Exclusive Breastfeeding at 6 Months in England Based on the 2024 Infant Feeding Survey
articles.abstract: The 2024 Infant Feeding Survey likely overestimates exclusive breastfeeding prevalence at 6 months in England. Roughly correcting for probable selection and attrition bias, true prevalence is more plausibly in the region of 4–17%, with an upper bound estimate of 21.4%. More precise estimates would require individual level data, which would allow formal modelling and direct estimation of differential attrition by feeding status.

articles.title: The Growing Transatlantic Sanctions Divide
articles.abstract: Multilateral cooperation on sanctions is a key determinant of their success, yet transatlantic collaboration on sanctions is steeply declining. This transatlantic sanctions divide is a symptom of increasingly divergent US and EU foreign policies. Sanctions are likewise best terminated multilaterally to effectively wield them as leverage. Here too, trustful US-EU collaboration is increasingly difficult to imagine. Nonetheless, strong public support for sanctioning Russia in both the EU and US offers a basis for continuing forceful Western sanctions as Russia escalates its war of aggression against Ukraine.

articles.title: Generative AI and Society
articles.authors: Laura K. Nelson, Daniel Karell, Thomas Davidson
articles.abstract: For sociologists, generative AI inherits the legacy of earlier computational technologies: it is an advancement of machine learning already adopted as a methodology, and it intervenes in a society already shaped by algorithmic systems. Yet it also has a dimension that distinguishes it from previous computational methods, and one that makes it inherently sociological: its interactivity. In this review, we conceptualize the interactivity of generative AI and introduce a framework for understanding how it operates across individual, organizational, and institutional life. Specifically, the framework specifies how generative AI expands users, functions as a proxy for society, and expresses power, both in sociological practice and in society. We conclude by suggesting three dynamics driven by generative AI that sociology will face in the near future: the transformation of scientific practice, the reorganization of social interaction, and the acceleration of algorithmic governance.

articles.title: Able but unwilling? Mapping citizens’ political GenAI use through the lens of Expectancy-Value Theory
articles.authors: Michael van Straelen, Christopher Starke, Patrick van Erkel, Jessica Piotrowski, Nils Köbis
articles.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) holds promise and risk for democracy, yet little is known about how citizens evaluate and adopt it for political purposes. Drawing on Expectancy-Value Theory and Uses & Gratifications Theory, this study offers an initial account of political GenAI adoption, mapping how citizens' cost-value perceptions and expectancy beliefs cluster into distinct profiles. We investigate how these ‘expectancy-value profiles’ shape political GenAI use. Using cross-sectional survey data from 947 Dutch respondents, we conduct a latent profile analysis, identifying four profiles: optimists, cautious pragmatists, sceptics, and indifferents. Profile differences stem largely from differing cost-value perceptions rather than expectancy beliefs, suggesting the question is less about whether people feel able to use GenAI, and more about whether they feel it is worth using. Across all profiles, cost perceptions are high and political use is low, though optimists report significantly more use than others. Individuals’ political dispositions predict usage but not profile membership and among technological dispositions, trust in GenAI and belief in the machine heuristic predict being an optimist. Findings raise concerns about uncalibrated trust among adopters.

articles.title: A Stacked Deck: Ambition, Supply, Demand, and Women’s Access to Political Power
articles.authors: Mirya Holman, Lakshmi Iyer, Christina Wolbrecht
articles.abstract: Why do women remain underrepresented in positions of political power? A central challenge to answering this question is the difficulty in disentangling possible explanations, including women’s lack of interest or ambition, differences in women’s preparedness for political office, and discrimination against women by selectors. In this paper, we are uniquely able to investigate all three kinds of explanations simultaneously. Our unique dataset of applicants to appointed boards at the local level in the United States contains detailed professional, civic, and political information about the applicants, as well as about the boards to which they apply and the decisions of the appointers. We find that women are indeed less likely to apply for political positions, particularly powerful positions. The men and women who do apply are equally qualified. Despite these qualifications, women are less likely to be appointed to boards with more authority and power.

articles.title: Turning Votes into Power: New Women Voters and Access to Local Governance
articles.authors: Mirya Holman, Christina Wolbrecht, Lakshmi Iyer
articles.abstract: Do voting rights secure access to political power for previously excluded groups? We theorize that organizational capacity and ideological congruence with political regimes determine whether voting rights produce access to governance. We test this theory with the case of American women’s suffrage and a new measure of access to power: representation on local appointed boards. Using a new dataset of more than 30,000 appointees, hundreds of women’s organizations, and local political regimes in four major cities, we find that suffrage facilitates descriptive representation, but this connection is limited to when women are ideologically aligned with the political regime. Strength of women’s organizations is associated with women’s representation, but only before suffrage. Women’s representation remained concentrated on boards concerning children, arts, and welfare. Even with the vote, women’s access to governance depended on the preferences of the established male elite.

articles.title: Pre-modern checks and balances: an analysis of hunter-gatherer cultures
articles.authors: Honorata Mazepus, Natália Kubalová, Alexander Mangun, Elena Cecconi
articles.abstract: Although support for democratic values remains high across the world, political scientists report the erosion of institutional checks and balances. Why do citizens allow dismantling of democratic institutions? Does it mean that contemporary institutions for constraining authorities do not resonate with our human minds? In this paper we take the first steps to identify the pre-modern "original" mechanisms to constrain and empower authorities by investigating hunter-gatherer communities. Through the analysis of ethnographic records in the eHRAF World Cultures database, we examine (1) under what conditions hunter-gatherers empowered and constrained their leaders and (2) what mechanisms they used to prevent the abuse of power. In this pilot study, we analysed 1,106 paragraphs describing six cultures from different regions of the world and with different socio-political organization. Our analyses point to a set of possible political intuitions triggered by the challenges faced by a subset of hunter-gatherer communities. Preliminary findings show aversion towards domination, vigilance and punishment of rule violations, preference for competence-based leadership and majority decision-making. Our results suggest that democratic backsliding might not be due to the general incompatibility of checks and balances with the human intuitions about politics, but rather that the combination of the design of our institutions and the specific circumstances might enable democratic erosion.

articles.title: Rethinking Informational Privacy – Measurement and Validation of a General Informational Privacy Attitudes (GIPA) Scale
articles.authors: Robert Neumann, Hagen von Hermanni, Guido Mehlkop
articles.abstract: This study presents a novel measurement for privacy attitudes based on a three-component attitude model. Our theoretical approach treats privacy as a fundamental right along a negative conception and treats concerns about privacy violations as the key attitudinal components that are predictive for privacy-related behavior. We offer an alternative to existing measures focused on concerns and attitudes towards specific data use cases. Using survey data from Germany to develop the six-item GIPA scale, we apply the measure in a three-country survey covering the U.S., India, and Germany where we validate the scale with respect to measurement invariance and convergent validity. Results demonstrate good model fit, metric measurement invariance across countries, and predictive validity in relation to COVID-19 tracing app usage and digital payment app acceptance.

articles.title: Examining Rising Life Satisfaction in Russia Amidst War: The Role of Perceived Socioeconomic Status Before and During the Ukraine War
articles.abstract: Previous research has firmly established life satisfaction within the Russia Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS) as a reliable measure for assessing perceived quality of life within Russia. In this paper, we present perceived socioeconomic status (PSS) within the RLMS as a latent measure introduced to help examine levels of life satisfaction in Russia before (prewar 2018-2019) and during the Ukraine war (wartime 2022-2023). Using exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and structural equation modelling (SEM), the findings indicate that PSS is a robust measure that increases the explanatory power of prewar and wartime models and positively predicts life satisfaction in both periods. Contemporary wellbeing research consistently supports the view that a key mechanism in shaping life satisfaction lies in how certain demographic conditions are psychologically interpreted. Drawing on appraisal theory, the study thus suggests that subjective appraisals of socioeconomic position provide meaningful information for understanding wellbeing that cannot be captured by demographic characteristics alone. Moreover, in the RLMS, overreliance on demographic indicators is shown to obscure the subjective mechanisms through which individuals living through wartime conditions evaluate their life satisfaction and interpret their social positions. Overall, the paper emphasizes that future research on the RLMS should consider incorporating PSS in their analyses and further developing on how subjective appraisals of socioeconomic position capture aspects of life satisfaction that are simply immeasurable in demographic only models of the RLMS. Emphasis should be placed on the major social, economic, and political disruption caused by the war that become normalized over time.

articles.title: The Changing Gender Training Gap - A Systematic Review of Evidence from Germany
articles.abstract: Research on gender differences in non-formal job-related further training in Germany has produced inconsistent findings, leaving unclear how gender inequalities in training have developed and whether divergent findings reflect training forms or conceptual and meth-odological differences. This systematic review synthesised quantitative evidence from studies published between 1990 and 2026. Web of Science, Scopus, and FIS Bildung were searched in June 2026 and supplemented by backward citation searching. Forty-two stud-ies yielded 160 finding-level records, which were integrated using a structured narrative synthesis. The evidence indicates a weakening of the earlier male advantage in overall training participation, with later evidence increasingly showing no statistically detectable gender difference or higher participation among women. This convergence was weaker for employer-supported training, while population-level convergence coexisted with life-course-specific inequalities. Conceptual and methodological differences shaped the com-parability and empirical visibility of gender inequalities but did not systematically ac-count for the broader historical pattern, which remained visible under more restrictive comparisons. Overall, gender inequality in further training appears to have been recon-figured rather than eliminated or simply reversed, with inequalities remaining conditional on institutional and life-course contexts.

articles.title: How bibliometric indicators align with REF 2021 peer review across disciplines
articles.abstract: Bibliometric indicators are increasingly used to approximate expert peer review, but how well they do so varies across disciplines in ways that remain poorly understood. Existing analyses of the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) have largely correlated metrics with individual article quality scores, within single fields and using restricted-access data. This study takes a complementary approach based on publicly available data: institutional REF 2021 output GPA is correlated with a consistent set of citation-based and journal-based indicators for all submitting institutions across fifteen Units of Assessment (UoAs). Comparing the two types of indicators side by side reveals a continuum of evaluation cultures. At one end, Physics tracks citation impact far more closely than journal rank (correlations of 0.85 versus 0.42, based on the share of outputs in the top 10% of each measure). At the other end, Business and Management Studies shows the reverse (0.59 versus 0.92), among the strongest journal-based correlations across all fields examined. Of the fifteen UoAs, nine correspond best with journal-based indicators and six with citation-based indicators, a divide that cuts across the usual STEM/non-STEM boundary. Indicator validity is therefore not a property of the metric alone but of the discipline’s evaluation culture, and research assessment should choose and interpret metrics field by field.

articles.title: Modeling Network Dynamics with Overlapping Cohesive Subgroups
articles.authors: Stepan Zaretckii, Tom A.B. Snijders, Marijtje A.J. van Duijn, Christian Steglich
articles.abstract: We introduce a longitudinal extension of the latent membership stochastic actor-oriented model (LM-SAOM) for analyzing the co-evolution of network ties and actors’ memberships in overlapping cohesive subgroups. The model treats group memberships as latent and time-evolving, giving actors frequent opportunities to update their memberships while a strong \emph{membership cohesion} effect favors membership choices that place actors in the same groups as their network contacts, thereby keeping the inferred cohesive subgroups aligned with the evolving network. In an application to a friendship network, we find evidence that students are more likely to have ties with peers with whom they share cohesive subgroup membership, beyond what is captured by dyadic and triadic effects. Goodness-of-fit assessments indicate that incorporating group-level dependence improves the representation of selected meso-level network configurations.

articles.title: Learning to Speak Green: The Production of Green Conformity in European Cultural Policy
articles.authors: Vânia Rodrigues, Catarina Santos-Silva, Olga Solovova
articles.abstract: Ecological vocabulary is nearly absent until 2021, when greening became a cross-cutting programme priority, and rises abruptly thereafter. Green, climate and sustainable increasingly appear together as an interchangeable signal of commitment. Sustainable also retains its earlier organisational meaning, binding ecological claims to claims of institutional survival. Modernisation dominates the coded projects, framing sustainability as innovation, capacity-building and better practice. Transformative elements persist only as traces, and the vocabularies of degrowth, commoning and ecological justice are absent or residual across the whole corpus. The programme's explicit greening guidance appears to supply the very terms in which compliance is demonstrated. The article argues that this narrowing is anticipatory and sincere, which makes it harder to contest than greenwashing. It contributes to debates on travelling cultural policy and multilateral cultural governance by showing how a transnational green idiom, composed largely in English, carries a sustainability paradigm across Europe while constraining the ecological futures cultural institutions can meaningfully articulate.

articles.title: Uncovering the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth: an interdisciplinary review and research agenda
articles.authors: Franziska Cooiman, Julia de Groote, Isabell Stamm, Jan Ole Krieg
articles.abstract: Given the centrality of entrepreneurial activity to the accumulation, reproduction, and legitimization of wealth – and conversely, of wealth in the form of capital to foster entrepreneurship – it might be reasonable to expect a plethora of research on the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth. However, as we demonstrate in our interdisciplinary literature review, a surprising lack of engagement exists with regard to this relationship. Sociological studies of wealth inequality rarely address entrepreneurship, and entrepreneurship research rarely addresses wealth. We systematically review, discuss, and synthesize the discourse in the leading journals of both fields. In the sociological discourse on wealth, we find that entrepreneurship is seen as one of many sources of income and wealth, and as a means of legitimizing its accumulation. However, the social practices, actors, and institutions that mediate the concentration of wealth through entrepreneurship, as well as the structural power of wealth in entrepreneurial activity, are rarely addressed. Similarly, in entrepreneurship research, we show that considerable attention is paid to the role of family businesses, transgenerational wealth, and non-financial wealth (“socioemotional wealth”), whilst the fundamental role of these factors in fostering wealth concentration more broadly remains largely unremarked upon in the literature. We therefore suggest future research that systematically engages with how entrepreneurial activity shapes wealth accumulation, and how wealth, in turn, structures entrepreneurial opportunities and outcomes. With this review, we contribute to advancing debates on inequality, social mobility, and economic development.

articles.title: Global Trends in Widowhood Prevalence, 1970–2020: The Role of Population Ageing, Mortality, and Union Dynamics
articles.abstract: Widowhood is the predominant marital status at older ages, especially among women. Although population ageing is expected to increase widowhood, evidence on this trend remains scarce or fragmented across countries. This study contributes to the global understanding of widowhood by addressing two questions. First, how has widowhood prevalence changed among women and men across countries and world regions between 1970 and 2020? Second, to what extent are changes in overall widowhood prevalence attributable to changes in population age structure rather than to changes in age-specific widowhood prevalence, i.e. mortality and union dynamics. We gathered marital-status tabulations from censuses, registers, and nationally representative surveys covering 222 countries and territories, and trace crude and age-standardized widowhood prevalence from 1970 to 2020. A Kitagawa decomposition separates change between 1980 and 2010 in 135 populations into age-structure and age-specific-prevalence components. Widowhood prevalence declined globally and in most regions, especially among women. Although population ageing contributed to increasing widowhood prevalence, changes in age-specific prevalence more than offset this effect. An ageing world is not necessarily one in which an increasing share of people are widowed, but it may still be one in which large, socially vulnerable populations live with the consequences of spousal loss.

articles.title: Unbundling Support for Political Violence
articles.authors: Sam Fuller, Jack T. Rametta, Alexa Federice
articles.abstract: Measures of support for political violence (SPV) vary drastically across what violence they describe, who performs it, against whom, and the stated justification. We argue that these measures are not interchangeable operationalizations of a single latent attitude but rather represent correlated, distinct subdimensions of SPV. Across three studies, we iteratively develop and validate concise batteries that 1) differentiate between actor-target combinations and reactive versus proactive violence and 2) vary across justification and the response's severity. We find that SPV is a multidimensional concept: levels of reactive support are remarkably higher than proactive; support for state-on-mass and mass-on-state violence are only weakly correlated, with Republicans supporting state-on-mass and Democrats supporting mass-on-state violence at significantly higher rates; common SPV measures correlate with proactive more than reactive; and we find mixed evidence that survey disengagement influences SPV. Our findings contextualize disparate and conflicting literatures, offering measurement strategies tailored to specific research questions.

articles.title: Long-Term Health Financing in Chile: A Historical Analysis of the Segmented System, 1981–2024

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: The objective of this article is to present the results of reconstructing the historical series of health expenditure in Chile from the creation of the segmented model in 1981 to 2024, and to briefly analyze its evolution in historical context. To this end, data were collected and digitized from primary sources: the Statistical Bulletins and Public Accounts of FONASA (1989–2016; 2020–2024), the Statistical Series of the Isapre System (SUPER, 1990–2024), and the Public Finance Statistics of DIPRES (2004–2025). The results show accelerated growth in private spending until the 1990s, followed by a sustained increase in public health expenditure associated with higher fiscal contributions and mandatory contributions. However, the long-term analysis reveals periods of slowdown in public spending coinciding with the expansion of private infrastructure, revealing the persistence of a segmented and unequal financing system. The trajectory of Chilean health expenditure shows significant variation in proportions and pace, conditioned by political and economic contexts. Alongside this analysis, we make the complete series used available to researchers in open access.

articles.title: Quo Vadis, Digital Accessibility? A Prerequisite for Democratic Equality
articles.authors: Tânia de Jesus Vilela da Rocha, Gonçalo Alexandre Cruz Conde de Matos

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Digital participation channels may widen access to public decision-making, but formal availability does not ensure substantively equal opportunities for political voice. This paper asks how accessibility conditions across a digital consultation journey may shape participation costs and what their potential implications are for political equality and procedural legitimacy. It conceptualizes digital accessibility as democratic infrastructure and integrates technical accessibility, journey analysis, socio-technical evaluation, and democratic interpretation. The analytical strategy distinguishes observed conditions, plausible participation risks, and demonstrated outcomes and traces a chain from observed condition to required resource, participation cost, recovery route, and potential democratic relevance. A bounded exploratory pilot applies the strategy to the publicly accessible, logged-out segment of ConsultaLEX, the Portuguese government portal for legislative and regulatory consultations. The pilot covers discovery, orientation, and authentication and assesses the availability of an entry point to expression and feedback. It identifies enabling conditions in programmatically named controls, structured consultation information, exact dates, and alternative authentication routes. Potentially constraining conditions involve relative deadlines, scripted navigation, registration and identity requirements, and human verification. Because no live commenting process was available, expression and feedback could not be inspected. The study therefore supports mechanism-level inferences rather than claims about participant exclusion or platform-wide conformance. These findings support treating accessibility as a necessary but insufficient condition for equal participation. The paper contributes a proof of concept connecting accessibility evidence to democratic analysis and identifies disability-led participant testing, live-process observation, and cross-platform comparison as priorities for future research.

articles.title: Specific Support, Diffuse Trust: Central Banks and the Mass Politics of Unconventional Monetary Policy
articles.abstract: Central banks relied for a decade on unconventional monetary policies (negative interest rates, large-scale asset purchases, and forward guidance) that carry significant distributive consequences and became intensely politicized. Yet little is known about the mass politics of central banking, or whether contestation over specific instruments threatens central banks' broader legitimacy. We provide evidence from two pre-registered survey experiments in Germany and the Netherlands. A conjoint experiment shows that citizens strongly oppose negative interest rates, the most penalized levels in the design, and are skeptical of unconditional asset purchases. A framing experiment shows support for negative rates responds to both egotropic and sociotropic arguments, with pocketbook concerns resonating most strongly. Exploiting a within-respondent measure of trust in the European Central Bank (ECB), we show that these same frames shift citizens' specific support for the policy without eroding their diffuse trust in the ECB, a highly insulated, technocratic, non-elected institution.
