articles.title: What’s Worth Dreaming of? The Gendered and Classed Logics Behind Occupational Aspirations
articles.abstract: Even though occupations have multiple characteristics that make them more or less likely to be aspired to, research has yet to capture which characteristics matter most for which adolescents. This limits our understanding of inequalities in aspirations because different theories emphasize the role of certain occupational characteristics over others. This article examines whether and how evaluations of multiple characteristics combine into distinct logics of aspirations based on adolescents’ gender, class, and gender-class intersection. We combine Swiss data from the DAB Panel Study on adolescents’ aspirations with O*NET data on occupational characteristics. Using conditional logit models, we estimate the relationships between occupational characteristics and the choice of aspired occupation. Results show that girls prioritize occupations satisfying female-typed interests and those requiring higher education levels, while boys avoid occupations with high shares of women and high educational requirements. High-class adolescents favour artistic and investigative occupations, whereas low-class adolescents are averse to highly educated and high-income occupations. Intersectional analyses reveal that low-class boys are particularly disadvantaged, exhibiting the strongest aversion to highly educated occupations. Overall, findings highlight that aspirations are shaped by multiple occupational characteristics rather than a single dimension, underscoring the importance of a multidimensional perspective to better understand inequalities in adolescent aspirations.

articles.title: Staged financing beyond the venture record: Equity rounds in the accounts of Italian SMEs
articles.authors: Angelo Leogrande, Mauro di Molfetta, Valeria Notarnicola, Maria Giovanna Trotta, Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles.abstract: Almost everything known about equity rounds in young firms comes from the records of professional investors, so the evidence is selected on the presence of an intermediary. We read rounds instead from the share-premium reserve, a compulsory, disclosed and restricted line of the Italian statutory balance sheet, for 3,225 certified innovative SMEs over 2016–2025: 2,991 priced capital increases on 1,330 firms. Firms about to raise grew twice as fast in the preceding year and held identical cash, yet six in ten closed it at a loss; profitability falls and intangible assets rise only after the round. Seven panel estimators place the association across firms and not within them; a taxonomy estimated blind to the event finds the mechanism in all five financial configurations, with incidence differing eightfold; six flexible learners fail to improve on the linear specification. Selection operates on growth, not on profitability, a distinction intermediated samples cannot see.

articles.title: Harnessing Human–AI Interpretive Difference: Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism
articles.abstract: Recent debate over GenAI in qualitative inquiry centres on concerns that computational participation reinforces postpositivist dominance. Critical analysts propose excluding it, out-theorising it, or continuously inspecting its entanglements. In parallel, a growing body of work builds architectures to accommodate human-AI collaboration in interpretive inquiry. While most of this work relies on postpositivist assumptions, an emerging strand develops collaborative architectures grounded in interpretivism, an approach this article adopts. I propose that for computational interpretation to be part of interpretivist inquiry without being granted reflexivity or interpretive authority, it must be deliberately structured into an accountable, productive relationship alongside human interpretation. To that end, I outline Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism, an epistemological position resting on five propositions. First, productive epistemic non-equivalence holds that human and computational interpretation need not share an epistemic basis for their difference to be structured as a resource. Second, interpretive co-construction grounds computational interpretation in meanings negotiated between researcher and participant, rather than a decontextualised corpus. Third, productive divergence treats non-alignment between human and computational interpretations as a potential source of analytic insight. Fourth, interpretive traceability refers to the capacity to see the grounds upon which human and computational interpretations are made, rendering them accountable structurally. Fifth, reflexive engagement holds that computational participation can create occasions for the researcher to interrogate her relationship to her subjectivity. This position is operationalised through Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis (LICA). LICA deploys computational interpretation to anchor interpretive insights to the empirical material. It integrates explicit interpretive co-construction between participant and researcher in interviews, scrutinises divergence between researcher and computational interpretations, renders analytic reasoning traceable, and embeds the researcher's subjectivity into the computational process. Together, these features create the conditions for new insights to emerge from the interaction between human and computational interpretations.

articles.title: Do genes modify earnings trajectories following job loss? Gene-environment interactions with endogenous and exogenous forms of job loss
articles.authors: INVEST Flagship, Arno Van Hootegem, Henri Salokangas, Gaia Ghirardi, Henrik Dobewall, Laura Jernström, Maria Vaalavuo
articles.abstract: Job loss is a disruptive event that results in long-term economic scarring, though effects vary across social groups. This study explores a new potential source of inequality in the impact of job loss by examining whether genetic traits can amplify or attenuate earning declines following job loss. To address bias from gene-environment correlations, we compare interactions between polygenic indices (PGIs) and both endogenous job loss (individual unemployment) and exogenous job loss (plant closures). We focus on PGIs for depression, educational attainment, and risk-taking. Using Finnish population register data linked to genetic information for approximately 10,000 individuals observed over ten years, we apply a difference-in-differences design. We find persistent earnings losses following job loss, with larger declines for endogenous unemployment spells. Genetic moderation is observed only for plant closures: individuals with higher depression-related PGIs experience greater earnings declines. No comparable interactions emerge for endogenous job loss or the other PGIs.

articles.title: From Working Life to Retirement: Changing Educational Inequalities in Income Trajectories in Germany
articles.abstract: Previous literature has mainly focussed on either income trajectories of higher education graduates in working life or in retirement. This paper advances this literature by investigates the inequalities of income trajectories at the transition into retirement and compare the trajectories to other educational graduates for the case of Germany. While cumulative advantage theory suggests that education-based income inequalities widen throughout working life, the institutional design of the German pension system fundamentally alters these trajectories. Using data from 1,741 (11,740 observations) baby boomers from the German Socio-Economic Panel Study (SOEP) I combine descriptive income trajectories with fixed effects regression and replacement rate analysis. find a stratified pattern by educational degree in pre- and post-retirement income. However, income inequality by education degree is more pronounced during work life than in retirement: At the transition into retirement income differences are compressed relative to pre-retirement disparities. This compression operates through heterogeneous replacement rates. Higher educated individuals have lower replacement rates than the rest of the educational groups. Germany’s contribution-capped statutory pension system therefore constitutes a structurally induced erosion of the income advantage that higher education generates over a working lifetime.

articles.title: Selection, Allocation, and Timing: Three Obstacles to Measuring the Effect of Large-Load Growth on Household Electricity Prices
articles.abstract: Published estimates of how hyperscale computing load affects household electricity prices disagree about sign as well as magnitude. This article argues that much of the disagreement reflects three identification problems that existing designs often absorb rather than model directly. Large loads choose low-cost locations, making exposure endogenous. Average revenue per kilowatt-hour cannot distinguish a change in rates from a change in the composition of customers within a class. In jurisdictions that allow construction costs into rates before a plant enters service, bills may change years before the associated load appears in sales data. I examine each problem using public data. With state-level price and sales data for 2023 and 2024 for the 50 states and the District of Columbia, I find direct evidence of siting selection: the 2023 residential price level explains 22 percent of the cross-state variance in subsequent non-residential sales growth. That sorting appears to follow a state’s general cost level rather than the depth of the discount already received by large customers, a more tractable pattern for identification. Non-residential sales growth has no detectable relation to residential price growth, although the design lacks power to detect elasticities below roughly 0.9, so the null is not substantively informative. The residential-to-industrial price ratio rises with load growth, but decomposition shows that seven-tenths of the movement comes from falling non-residential prices rather than rising residential prices; the same pattern appears relative to the commercial class, and half of the association disappears after adding a four-category regional control. Translating the reduced-form slope into an implied price for incremental load shows that a pure composition account would require these kilowatt-hours to be served at about one-third of the class average, a demanding but possible figure whose confidence interval cannot adjudicate the issue. The evidence favors a regime-dependent interpretation of the literature and indicates that future work should treat capital deployment, rather than realized energy sales, as the central treatment variable.

articles.title: Automated Creativity in the Imagined Network: Creative Writer's View on Generative AI
articles.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies reshape the creative sector, understanding their implications for writers becomes increasingly vital. The study addresses a significant research gap by the impact of GenAI on creative writers in the United Kingdom, focusing on their perceptions and interactions within professional networks. The research explores two primary questions: how UK creative writers perceive and interact with GenAI technologies in their professional network, and what factors shape these perceptions and interactions within the creative industry. Employing a qualitative approach, the study conducts in-depth interviews with members of the Writers' Guild of Great Britain to gather rich, contextual qualitative response. Key findings reveal the complex relationship between writers' self-identification within their professional networks and the integration of GenAI technologies. The study also uncovers writers' concerns about potential displacement by AI and examines the interplay between GenAI and capitalist forces in the creative industry. By centring the voices of creative writers, this research contributes to the ongoing discourse on technology and creativity, advocating for a more nuanced understanding of the sociotechnical dynamics in the creative industry. The study informs future discussions on the ethical use of AI in creative fields and provides an STS perspective on the evolving relationship between technology and creative professionals.

articles.title: Localizing the Sustainable Development Goals through Digitally Visible Initiatives: An Exploratory Study in Brazil
articles.authors: Cecilia Kotzias, Tamer Uzun, Hans Michael van Bellen, Roberto Pacheco, Cinthya Mônica da Silva Zanuzzi, Paulo Maurício Selig

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Community-based and other sustainability-oriented initiatives across Brazil address problems central to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), yet their contributions may be less visible within formal SDG monitoring because they are distributed across numerous small actors and often expressed in local rather than SDG terminology. This study frames the challenge of making the contributions of such initiatives legible within SDG localization as a knowledge-translation problem and develops an exploratory digital mapping and classification procedure for identifying and interpreting digitally visible sustainability-oriented initiatives in relation to nationalized SDG targets. An iterative snowball mapping procedure on Instagram identified 2,328 publicly visible profiles, from which 256 sustainability-oriented initiatives were classified in relation to nationalized SDG targets (230 assigned a primary SDG). A documented subset of 50 initiatives, including 47 examined using additional public sources, was analyzed in depth. Coding followed a transparent codebook, and an independent second coder recoded the documented subset, yielding moderate intercoder reliability (Cohen's κ = 0.57), followed by negotiated adjudication of disagreements. The findings indicate that many initiatives address SDG-relevant problems without using SDG terminology, that assigning a single primary SDG entails interpretive loss when representing multidimensional local practices, and that fewer than one quarter of the initiatives in the in-depth subset are directly recognized in Brazil's official civil society registry. The study introduces a transparent and auditable mapping-and-classification procedure grounded in this framing and provides empirical insights into both the analytical potential and the interpretive limits of translating situated local narratives into classifications aligned with nationalized SDG targets.

articles.title: No Reform, No Election: CHADEMA's Campaign and the Legacy of Incomplete Political Reform in Tanzania, 1991–2025
articles.abstract: On 23 March 2025, the Chama cha Demokrasia na Maendeleo (CHADEMA) launched its “No Reform, No Election” campaign in Mbeya City, demanding substantive electoral and political reforms as a condition for participation in Tanzania's forthcoming general election. Although the campaign emerged in the immediate aftermath of the 2024 local-government elections, its political rationale was rooted in a much longer history of incomplete institutional reform dating from the Nyalali Commission of 1991. This article examines the campaign within the historical trajectory of Tanzania's major presidential commissions and reform initiatives, including the Nyalali Commission, the Warioba Commission on corruption, the Kisanga Committee, the Warioba Constitutional Review Commission, and the Presidential Taskforce on Multiparty Democracy chaired by Professor Rwekaza Mukandala. The article argues that Tanzania's reform trajectory is characterized by a recurring gap between the identification of institutional problems, the production of reform recommendations, and their comprehensive implementation. This article conceptualizes this phenomenon as the reform implementation gap and argues that its cumulative effect has generated a reform expectation gap between citizens' and political actors' expectations and the institutional outcomes delivered by successive governments. The 2025 CHADEMA campaign should therefore be understood not simply as an electoral boycott strategy but as a political claim concerning the relationship between electoral participation and institutional legitimacy. The article further examines the 2023–2024 electoral and political-party legislation, CHADEMA's invocation of President Samia Suluhu Hassan's “4Rs” philosophy, and the opposition's increasing reliance on digital mobilization in a constrained political environment. It concludes that democratic consolidation in Tanzania requires not merely additional reform initiatives but credible implementation of existing recommendations, stronger institutional independence, and political conditions capable of sustaining meaningful electoral competition.

articles.title: Lexical Integration: Introducing Aymara Corpus Evidence into Global English
articles.abstract: Indigenous Andean languages have traditionally been preserved through oral traditions, especially following the historical destruction of non-alphabetic record-keeping systems like khipus (Coletta, 2023). In the face of imperial linguistic hegemony, traditional documentation efforts often prove insufficient for long-term epistemic preservation (van den Berg, 2024). As Global English expands, the decline of Indigenous languages threatens profound Andean ways of knowing with systematic erosion (van den Berg, 2024). This paper proposes a conceptual framework to preserve Highland Andean epistemology by integrating targeted, untranslatable Aymara words—such as ch’ixi, taypi, and suma qamaña—into Global English lexicons using international corpus evidence (Bosch & Griesel, 2020). Anchored in translanguaging theory and decolonial macro- and microethics, this approach maps translational deficiencies where English lacks single-word equivalents for complex Andean concepts. The study demonstrates that bridging these lexical gaps transforms Global English into an additive vehicle for cultural preservation, counteracting academic extractivism and projecting Indigenous philosophies onto the global stage.

articles.title: FASTrack: A co-designed cloud-based planning support system for interactive cycling infrastructure scenario assessment
articles.authors: Ryan Turner, Afshin Jafari, Sapan Tiwari, Alan Both, Dhirendra Singh, Steve Pemberton, Chris De Gruyter

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Testing transport interventions using city-scale transport models is typically resource intensive, requiring specialist expertise, substantial data and computational capacity. As a result, such modelling is often concentrated on major projects and larger metropolitan areas, while smaller interventions and mid-sized regional cities have limited access to comparable modelling capabilities. This is particularly relevant to active travel, where cycling infrastructure decisions frequently need to be made with relatively limited modelling and decision-support capacity. This study presents FASTrack, a cloud-based planning support software system that integrates agent-based modelling, behavioural simulation, and interactive scenario visualisation to enable proposed cycling infrastructure assessment. A case study is applied to the City of Greater Bendigo, a mid-sized regional Australian city representative of the planning contexts that existing platforms often overlook. FASTrack was developed through a co-design process over three years with local government planning partners, to address the need to rapidly assess infrastructure scenarios, quantify changes in cycling demand and behaviour, and inform infrastructure planning and investment appraisal. These requirements underpin its design, including the use of probabilistic modelling and a cloud-based workflow designed to support rapid, on-demand scenario testing with minimal specialist modelling expertise. Scenario outcomes are presented through interactive dashboard-style interfaces that detail estimated changes in network use, level of traffic stress, mode shift, cycling usage, emissions, and cost-benefit analysis aligned with national appraisal guidelines. This study demonstrates how co-design can directly shape the development of planning support systems by translating practitioner requirements into accessible modelling platforms for cycling infrastructure planning

articles.title: Mapping the Discourse Network of Cervical Cancer Screening on Reddit: A Topic-Network Approach
articles.abstract: Online health communities are a primary venue where the public interprets cervical cancer screening, yet how peer discourse, which has no editorial authority, bundles screening concerns remains unclear. Drawing on network agenda setting (NAS), this study treats a peer community as a collective agenda-setter and asks how it organizes screening topics. This paper analyzes 9,851 posts and comments from seven women's-health subreddits (August 2025 to January 2026) using Latent Dirichlet Allocation and the Analysis of Topic Model Networks, with Spearman topic-loading similarity filtered to a significant backbone. Thirteen topics form three communities: a diagnostic-information agenda, an embodied exam-experience agenda, and a narrative-and-support agenda. Embodied, temporally anchored concerns hold them together: timing and bleeding, pelvic pain, and access carry the highest betweenness. Sentiment follows network position, with support positive and cancer risk negative. These findings extend NAS to agenda-less, peer-driven settings and map how health agendas emerge from the bottom up.

articles.title: Do AI Occupational-Exposure Scores Measure AI? AIOE and Eloundou (2024) Largely Capture Cognitive Content; Webb (2020) Does Not
articles.abstract: A growing empirical literature uses pre-built "AI occupational exposure" scores (most prominently the AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) index of Felten, Raj, and Seamans (2021) and the GPT-4 task-exposure measure of Eloundou et al. (2024)) as occupation-level treatments or predictors for AI's labor-market effects. We show that two of the most-cited scores, AIOE and Eloundou's GPT-4 measure, substantially re-label cognitive task content rather than capturing AI-specific exposure, a construct-validity problem that does not extend to a third, differently-built score (Webb 2020, patent-based). This note horse-races these three measures against transparent cognitive/manual task-content indices and the established Autor–Dorn Routine Task Intensity (RTI) measure. Across 773 occupations: (i) the ten-plus AI "applications" underlying AIOE collapse to a single factor (first principal component ≈ 88%); (ii) AIOE and Eloundou each correlate strongly with a cognitive-ability index (+0.85 / +0.70) and negatively with a manual-ability index (−0.91 / −0.83), correlate 0.86 with each other, but only moderately with RTI (−0.33 / −0.30): the confound is specifically cognitive ability level, not the classic routine-task polarization axis; (iii) each score's positive wage association reverses sign controlling for cognitive content but is barely affected by controlling for RTI; and (iv) the much-cited pre-ChatGPT "AI foresight" wage-divergence pattern collapses to near-zero under the cognitive control (not under the RTI control). Critically, this collapse is not universal: Webb's patent-text-overlap score is essentially uncorrelated with AIOE (r=0.03) and Eloundou (r=−0.03), only weakly related to cognitive content (r=0.13), and its modest wage associations do not reverse under cognitive control. The cognitive-content collapse is a signature of how a score is built: subjective crowd-relatedness ratings (AIOE) or LLM/human task judgments (Eloundou), not an inherent property of occupational AI-exposure measurement. Studies using relatedness- or judgment-based exposure scores should control for cognitive content and re-interpret accordingly; a patent-based measure is not shown here to have the same problem, though its own construct validity is untested.

articles.title: Demographic Segregation in Online Information Ecosystems
articles.abstract: Concern about online echo chambers rests on the premise that the internet sorts people by politics. Research on online ideological segregation has accordingly measured partisanship almost to the exclusion of other social divides, and has measured it mostly within news, which is a small share of online activity (Allen et al., 2020; Muise et al., 2022). Whether partisan segregation is distinctive has therefore rarely been tested against demographic segregation on equal terms. Using a 1.6-million-user Twitter/X panel linked to voter file records (July 2018 to May 2023), we measure age, gender, partisanship and geography with a Theil index, and race more briefly alongside them. First, partisanship is not the dominant division of online attention. When measured across Democrats, Republicans and Independents, partisan segregation over general sharing behaviour is roughly a third of demographic segregation, and age separates users more sharply than party even within news, the content category where partisan segregation is strongest and where the existing literature has looked almost exclusively. Second, segregation is built at the article level rather than the outlet level. People who differ on any social divide we measure converge on the same outlets and diverge on which stories they select from them, which places segregation downstream of the outlet choices that most audience-level research observes. Geography is the exception and segregates at the outlet level, as local news would predict. Third, the five-year decline in demographic segregation is produced by different mechanisms for different divides. Gender’s decline reflects almost entirely who left the platform, partisanship’s reflects how people changed, and age’s is an even mixture, so parallel aggregate trends can rest on unrelated causes. Online attention is segregated along social lines that are largely not political, at a level of granularity that outlet-based measures cannot observe. Existing estimates of partisan echo chambers describe a narrower and less distinctive phenomenon than the polarisation literature has assumed.

articles.title: Beyond the Road Network: A Three-Layer Multimodal Accessibility Framework for Island and Remote Settings
articles.authors: Weining Kan, Amber DeJohn, Kyusik Kim, David Van Riper
articles.abstract: The majority of transport accessibility studies rely on road networks to calculate travel costs. This approach penalizes regions like Alaska and Hawaii, where roads are not the only mode used to reach nearby communities. As a result, contexts such as these are typically excluded from accessibility research. To address this gap, we propose a three-layer routing method: layer 1 uses standard road routing; layer 2 adds commercial flights for places roads do not reach; layer 3 connects the remaining communities to the nearest airport by straight-line distance, for cases where there is not a road at all. We tested this method in Alaksa and Hawaii on 13 types of healthcare facilities using census block groups as the unit of analysis. Road-only routing misses a lot: depending on the service type, 10% to 44% of Alaska block groups have no reachable facility within three hours by road. Adding flights and snap-routing resolves most of these gaps, bringing coverage above 96% for most service types in both states. The improvement is largest for services with few facilities, like medical labs and imaging centers, where flight routing alone adds 18% to 32% more block groups. Fewer than 6% of block groups remain unreachable after applying the full method, with these communities constituting the most remote and unreachable. The framework is highly adaptable and only requires three inputs: (1) a remote region where the road network is disconnected, (2) flight or ferry time data, and (3) a road network for the local legs of the trip. This approach is generalizable for other isolated regions both in the United States or globally, and offers an opportunity to expand how traditional accessibility measures capture remote and isolated geographies.

articles.title: The Latin American Demographic Boom in Spain. Mass Immigration and Ethnic Convergence in a New Country of Immigration
articles.authors: Miguel González-Leonardo, Guillaume Marois, Elena Ambrosetti
articles.abstract: Since the late twentieth century, Spain has undergone a rapid transition from emigration to immigration country, receiving around 510,000 immigrants annually between 2000 and 2022, approximately half from Latin America. This transformation has substantially increased population diversity, yet less is known about how diversity develops in relatively new immigration countries compared with established destinations. We combine register data, a retrospective analysis of births by parental background and a multi-state cohort-component model to examine changes in population diversity between 2000 and 2022 and project its potential evolution to 2062. The results show a rapid transformation of Spain’s population composition. Between 2000 and 2022, the share of the population under 40 with a foreign background – defined by country of birth and parental origins – increased from 5% to 28%, while 13% had a Latin American background in 2022. Assuming that migration, fertility and ethnic-mixing patterns remain constant, the share of the population under 40 with a foreign background would exceed 65% by 2062, with those of Latin American background reaching 32%. These findings demonstrate that the demographic consequences of immigration extend beyond the growth of the foreign-born population, as births and ethnic mixing progressively reshape the Spanish-born population. The study highlights the importance of incorporating foreign family backgrounds when assessing population diversity and provides new evidence on how diversity may evolve across generations in a recent immigration country.

articles.title: The Dual Costs of Marriage and Expectation Mismatch: A Mechanism for Understanding Gender Conflict in Contemporary China
articles.abstract: Against the backdrop of a sustained decline in marriage and birth rates in China and intensifying gender tensions, traditional explanations centered on individual preferences or gender norms are insufficient to account for the structural mechanisms involved. Drawing on the economics of marriage and the family, this paper examines how rising costs of housing, weddings, bride price, childbearing, and education affect men's decisions to enter marriage, as well as how the expansion of higher education, the shortage of standardized professional employment, and the motherhood penalty shape women's opportunity costs associated with marriage. Building on these factors, together with declining expectations of economic growth, changing lifestyle expectations, and the rising utility of singlehood as an alternative, the paper proposes the “Dual Marriage Costs–Expectation Mismatch Integrated Model” (the Di Formula) and uses “marital surplus” to characterize the comprehensive net benefits of marriage relative to singlehood. The paper argues that contemporary gender relations in China involve more than a conflict of values, but separately rising direct marriage costs for men and opportunity costs for women, together with a widening structural mismatch between modernity-based expectations and real resource constraints. When marital surplus declines and eventually becomes negative, individually rational decisions to postpone or forgo marriage may, in aggregate, contribute to declining marriage and birth rates and intensified gender tensions. Marriage is therefore increasingly shifting from a traditional mechanism of family cooperation toward a high-cost, high-risk, long-term economic decision.

articles.title: apcbound: Bounding Age-Period-Cohort Effects in Stata
articles.abstract: Age-period-cohort analysis is complicated by the exact linear dependency between age, period, and cohort, which prevents the separate identification of their linear effects without additional assumptions. The bounding approach addresses this problem by replacing arbitrary point-identifying constraints with substantively motivated restrictions on the linear age, period, and cohort components. This article introduces apcbound, a Stata package that implements this approach. The package provides commands for describing age-period-cohort patterns, estimating identified nonlinear components and linear combinations, exploring alternative rotations, deriving bounded and semi-bounded solutions under user-specified assumptions, and visualizing the resulting identification regions. We illustrate the workflow using German data from the European Social Survey on years of education. A substantively plausible restriction that the age effect on educational attainment should be broadly nondecreasing is used to derive bounds on the otherwise unidentified linear components. The package facilitates transparent sensitivity analysis by showing how substantive assumptions translate into alternative admissible decompositions.

articles.title: Daily Team Behaviors as Predictors of Team Effectiveness Outcomes: Evidence from a Technology Entrepreneurship Incubator Program
articles.authors: Meg Small, Sally Dancer, Jonathan Wright, Blake A. Colaianne, Gillian Sommerville

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Team effectiveness in high-stakes, time-limited work contexts remains an underexplored area of organizational and applied psychology research. This study examined whether daily process behaviors—specifically team communication and collaboration—predict end-of-program team effectiveness outcomes in the context of an intensive, eight-week technology entrepreneurship incubator program. Participants were members of five start-up teams enrolled in the start-up program at a large research university. As part of a larger mixed-methods study, participants completed daily diary measures of team communication and collaboration using a digital platform (Metricwire) for 15 days. At program end, participants completed a post-program survey assessing team effectiveness outcomes including creativity, psychological safety, team viability, collective efficacy, authentic relationships, opportunities for growth, and program satisfaction. Simple linear regressions revealed that daily collaboration significantly predicted creativity, psychological safety, team viability, and collective efficacy. Daily communication similarly predicted creativity and psychological safety. Authentic relationships were not significantly predicted by either behavioral measure. These findings contribute to the growing literature on team process and performance by demonstrating that observable daily team behaviors capture meaningful variance in team effectiveness outcomes, Implications for team-based intervention design and digital measurement methodology are discussed.

articles.title: Who influences climate adaptation? Farmer and advisor social networks and differentiated benefits of participation in a climate adaptation fellowship program
articles.authors: Sara Delaney, Rachel E. Schattman, Janica Anderzén
articles.abstract: Due to ongoing and projected environmental change farmers and agricultural advisors need access to up-to-date and relevant information and advice to continue to be effective in their work. Education and advising services aim to transmit new information and facilitate change in behavior, often using peer-to-peer or cohort style approaches. However, given that learning and behavior is continuously shaped by interactions, we must understand the role of these interventions within broader climate adaptation networks. This study explores the social networks of a cohort of farmers and agricultural advisors who participated in a Climate Adaptation Fellowship program. Drawing on pre- and post-program surveys and interviews and longitudinal social network analysis, we first explore the range of sources that farmers and advisors in this cohort reported using for adaptation-related information, advice, and support. We also examine the impact of the program on the inter-cohort network and participants’ individual social networks. We find high diversity in the composition of interviewees’ adaptation networks. Farmers and advisors engage widely on adaptation, and while they use other farmers and advisors as resources for adaptation, they also draw on media, customers, friends, family, and the broader community. This heterogeneity has benefits for effective decision-making but also implies that messaging through single channels will only reach a limited audience. The analysis also shows that the program had variable effects among participants over time. There was a meaningful change in the social networks of approximately half of the fellows. While a subset of the group grew progressively more densely connected, others lost contact. We argue that this uneven engagement and impact is not a fault, but instead an invitation to capitalize on the energy of these most interconnected members and also find opportunities to engage those on the periphery over time. Programming can also be strategically expanded to a wider circle to help participants carry forward new learning.

articles.title: To a neo-patriarchy? How anti-gender backlash shapes the youth gender gap in populist radical right voting in the Netherlands
articles.abstract: Why are young European men more likely to vote for populist radical right parties (PRRPs) compared to young European women today? Following the concepts of cultural backlash and gender populism, we argue that anti-gender backlash, in the form of perceived status decline (PSD), opposition to gender diversity (OGD) and support for traditional gender roles (STGR), drives especially young men to PRRPs, in particular those who perceive threat from immigrants. We applied structural equation modelling on an 18–35-year-old subsample of the 2023 Dutch Parliamentary Election Study (N = 1,022). We find that the youth gender gap in PRRP voting can be explained by young men’s higher OGD, STGR, and unexpectedly also perceived threat from immigrants, but not by PSD. We conclude that gender differences in cultural backlash shape today’s youth gender gap in PRRP voting and might shape the future of European liberal democracy.

articles.title: Settler Colonial Logics: A framework for tracing the ideological currents of European colonisation of the Pacific
articles.abstract: This paper expands upon Patrick Wolfe’s ‘logic of elimination’ to propose a broader conceptual framework to understand the logics which underpinned European settler colonialism at large. Using the three Pacific voyages of British navigator James Cook between 1768 and 1779 as a case study, the geographic and ideological expansion of empire is positioned as a maritime endeavour which works to draw a singular geographic and political border for Empire. This view of a singular oceanic empire, rather than a collection of diverse and individual nations and peoples is further supported by the integration of the principles of the Doctrine of Discovery. This integration highlights the ways in which settler colonial logics continue to support structures founded on early modern beliefs about race, civilization and faith which, while now condemned by the institutions and cultures which established them, nonetheless continue to shape the lives of both Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in settler-colonial societies around the Pacific and beyond.

articles.title: Role of Industry 4.0 Technologies in Enhancing Supply Chain Resilience of Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs): A PLSSEM Based Empirical Investigation
articles.authors: Komal Sharma, Deepika Rathi, Dr Jainish Bhagat, RONAK AJAYKUMAR MEHTA
articles.abstract: Purpose – This study examines how the adoption of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies – the Internet of Things (IoT), Big Data Analytics (BDA), Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML), Blockchain (BCT), and Digital Twin (DTW) – influences the supply chain resilience (SCR) of Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), through the mediating roles of supply chain visibility (SCV), supply chain agility (SCA), and supply chain collaboration (SCC), and the moderating role of organizational readiness (ORGREAD). Design/methodology/approach – A structural model integrating the Resource-Based View and the Dynamic Capabilities View was tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) on survey data from 260 supply chain, operations, procurement, and digital-transformation executives in OEM firms across the automotive, electronics/electrical, industrial machinery, aerospace, and consumer-durables sectors. I4.0 technology adoption (I4ADOPT) is modelled as a second-order construct formed by five first-order technology dimensions; supply chain resilience is modelled as a second-order construct reflecting robustness, redundancy, flexibility, and recovery. The structural model was estimated with 2,000-sample nonparametric bootstrapping. Findings – I4ADOPT significantly and positively predicted SCV (β = 0.487, p < .001), SCA (β = 0.254, p < .001), and SCC (β = 0.193, p < .01), and exerted a significant direct effect on SCR (β = 0.175, p < .01). SCV, SCA, and SCC each significantly predicted SCR (β = 0.237, 0.354, and 0.240 respectively, all p < .001) and significantly, partially mediated the I4ADOPT–SCR relationship. SCV additionally strengthened both SCA (β = 0.335) and SCC (β = 0.308). Organizational readiness had a significant positive direct association with both SCV (β = 0.169) and SCA (β = 0.205), but its hypothesized moderating (interaction) effect on the I4ADOPT–SCV and I4ADOPT–SCA relationships was not statistically supported. The model explained 58.2% of the variance in supply chain resilience, and all measurement-model reliability, validity, and model-fit criteria were satisfied (SRMR = 0.013). Practical implications – OEM managers should prioritise IoT- and analytics-led visibility investment as the entry point of a digital resilience strategy, since visibility significantly amplifies agility and collaboration in addition to its own direct effect on resilience, and should invest in organizational readiness (leadership commitment, digital skills, process maturity) as a parallel, direct driver of these capabilities rather than solely as a moderating lever.

articles.title: Toward a sustainable post-pandemic growth
articles.abstract: This study investigates the long-run relationship between Research and Development (R&D) expenditure, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows, financial market capitalization, population, and Carbon Dioxide (CO2) emissions across five ASEAN economies–Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam– over 2000–2023. Building on the Paramati et al. (2021) framework rooted in the Impact, Population, Affluence, Technology (IPAT) theory of Ehrlich and Holdren (1971), the study applies Pedroni's panel cointegration test, the Pesaran (2007) CIPS unit-root test to address cross-sectional dependence, and Fully Modified OLS (FMOLS) estimation at both the panel and country-level. Results show that (i) population is the most consistently significant driver of CO2 emissions across all five economies, (ii) R&D expenditure carries a negative but statistically insignificant coefficient, a result consistent with the region's structurally low R&D-to-Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ratios and lagged green-technology effects (Yang et al., 2025; Mehmood et al., 2022), and (iii) FDI and financial-market effects are heterogeneous, supporting a Malaysia-Singapore green-finance interpretation alongside pollution-haven dynamics elsewhere. The findings highlight the need for ASEAN policymakers to scale R&D intensity, channel financial market deepening toward green sectors, and integrate demographic-driven emission pressures into national climate plans.

articles.title: From playing computer games to achieving lexical knowledge: Linking attitudes and time allocation with vocabulary acquisition
articles.abstract: The impact of video games on vocabulary acquisition has not received sufficient attention, despite a growing interest in the influence of digital games on vocabulary learning (i.e., DGVL) in the field of computer-assisted language learning (CALL). Particularly, it is uncertain whether the duration of time spent playing a video game and the attitude of English language learners (ELLs) have significant effects on EFL vocabulary acquisition. The present quasi-experimental study involved 40 male EFL students at a private language institute and examined the link between the students' opinions of a video game as well as the time allocated to it, in terms of vocabulary acquisition. In particular, this research explored the influence of these factors on receptive or productive vocabulary learning. Moreover, the vocabulary learning strategies employed by the participants when playing, along with the features they deemed essential for computer games to be engaging enough to support learning, were addressed in this study. The participants were required to complete a pretest, a posttest, a survey, and a self-reported timetable. The analyses did not reveal meaningful correlation between the participant's perception of the target video game and vocabulary acquisition. Additionally, it was found that the time spent playing the video game, coupled with prior language proficiency, helped to boost English vocabulary learning. Insights regarding the vocabulary learning strategies adopted and the features found appealing were also provided. These outcomes offer important insights for ESL/EFL instructors regarding the most effective approach to employing computer games as a novel vocabulary learning method. Keywords: Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL), Game-Enhanced Language Learning, Digital Game-Based Vocabulary Learning (DGVL), Computer games, Video Games, ESL/EFL pedagogy, TESOL, second language acquisition, Vocabulary Acquisition.

articles.title: The Electoral Effects of U.S. Prison Construction

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: From 1980 to 2000, the United States opened over 400 prisons, a rapid expansion of carceral capacity mirroring the punitive turn in public policy and public opinion. Yet few studies have examined the impact of prison construction on nearby residents and their political behavior. We develop a theoretical model tracing how prison openings affect economic, attitudinal, and electoral outcomes in surrounding communities. Using modern difference-in-difference methods and a novel county-level dataset covering forty years of prison openings, we find that prison construction decreases county-level vote share for Republican candidates, especially if Republicans represented the county during prison construction. Drawing on analyses of economic outcomes and prison bond measure support, we argue that voters sanction issue-owning Republican candidates for negative economic externalities and turn against funding for prisons. These findings challenge conventional wisdom about the political economy of prisons and have implications for how we understand contemporary expansions of carceral capacity.

articles.title: Concentration Without Representation
articles.abstract: A small fraction of users produces most of what circulates online, and the expectation that falling publication costs would flatten this gradient has not been borne out. Two questions about that concentration remain open. Published estimates of how concentrated sharing is vary by a factor of three at comparable thresholds, with no account of why, and the demographic composition of heavy sharers has received little systematic attention outside the study of misinformation, where existing work does not separate the users who share the most from those whose shares reach the most people. Using 38 million news shares by 493,237 registered US voters matched to their Twit- ter accounts across 57 months, we address both. Observation-window length alone reproduces the full factor-of-three range within a single dataset, holding population and content fixed. The top one percent accounts for 22 percent of shares at a one-week window and 52 percent at 57 months. Two tests establish that the rise is compositional and not behavioral, since holding sample size fixed does not flatten the curve and a cohort of the same users followed across all windows stays near 21 percent throughout. Matching observation windows to prior studies that overlap our own panel narrows the gap for comparable content almost entirely, while a residual gap against misinformation-specific estimates reflects a difference in content class rather than window choice. Ranking the same users by sharing volume and by audience reach identifies substantially overlap- ping but still distinct populations, overlapping by 49.9 percent at the top one percent against one percent expected by chance. Both elites are older and more Democratic than the panel, with mean age rising from 40.5 years to 57.0 under activity ranking. Gender behaves differently. Male and female users share at statistically indistinguishable rates throughout the activity distribution, and a thirteen-point gap appears only at the extreme of the follower tail, where female share falls to 34.8 percent. Elite position is durable at the head of the distribution and close to memoryless in the middle. The users who share the most only partly overlap with the users whose shares travel furthest, and both groups are unrepresentative of the voting public in overlapping but distinct ways.

articles.title: A Multicriteria Multimethod Analysis of Barriers for Green Infrastructure Implementation in Developing Countries: A Case Study of Sri Lanka
articles.authors: Udya Abeysinghe, Archana Sharma, Jagath Munasinghe

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Many developed economies are considering the use of Urban Green Infrastructure (UGI) as a tool to enhance the climate resilience of urban areas and align with SDG 11 - Make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable. Yet, the integration of UGI in developing countries seems to be lagging. Thus, they are missing out on one of the instruments that could facilitate developing nations’ compliance with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. This review examines the current state of UGI knowledge and implementation in Sri Lanka through a comprehensive literature review, an evaluation of UGI-related policies, guidelines, plans, and projects, and an assessment of stakeholder perspectives using the Delphi technique. As a result, the study identifies five significant challenges of mainstreaming UGI in Sri Lanka, such as lack of: clear consensual understanding of UGI- definition, ecosystem service functionality, implementation facilitative classification of UGI, design tool for UGI adaptation in constrained urban context, political willingness to integrate UGI planning principles in urban planning, robust legal framework and well-specified co-governance. Furthermore, the paper identifies concepts and tools as a forward path, such as a clear acknowledgement of current enabling conditions and gaps through known/ unknown diagram, categorization of multifunctional UGI such as with ecosystem service (ES) or place-making (PM) UGI, use of design syntax for adaptable design, and enhancement of regulatory framework. This review aspires to open the conversation on usefulness of UGI as a step towards climate resilience and SDG 11, at all levels of academic institutions to governmental agencies, in Sri Lanka. KEYWORDS: Urban Green Infrastructure (UGI), Nature-based Solutions (NbS), Climate Resilience, Sustainable Development Goal 11 (SDG 11), Urban Planning, Landscape, Design Syntax, Placemaking, Mixed method, Multimethod, Multicriteria, Analysis

articles.title: Review bombing the video game industries: Sabotage as political consumer practice
articles.abstract: Spaces of consumption have long been sites of tension and contestation between corporations and consumers. Since the late 2010s, review bombing has emerged as a persistent feature of this conflict. Consumers practice review bombing to take action in response to perceived grievances by inundating products with negative online reviews to drive down their aggregate ratings. Online reviews have been touted as part of a shift in power from producers to consumers championed by the logics of social commerce, and yet companies wield tremendous power over consumers. This study frames review bombing as sabotage, a withdrawal of efficiency. Through relational-ethnographic approaches to two cases of review bombing in the video game industries, the study argues that the efficacy of review bombing depends on a combination of spectacle and policy. While specific outcomes vary, review bombing is exceedingly effective at sabotaging the logics of the video games industries more broadly.

articles.title: Minimum Attainment Cost: National Benchmark Framework for Measuring Healthcare Accessibility in Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias-Related Services
articles.authors: Kyusik Kim, Amber DeJohn, Weining Kan

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: A threshold represented as travel time or distance is a key concept for determining catchment areas in cumulative opportunity and Two-Step Floating Catchment Area methods. As destinations included in a catchment area are determined by the threshold, it is a primary factor affecting spatial accessibility. In many cases, thresholds are arbitrarily determined or fixed values are used. The resulting accessibility based on these arbitrary or fixed thresholds makes it challenging to compare accessibility scores across heterogeneous geographic contexts (e.g., urban and rural areas). In this paper, we propose the Minimum Attainment Cost (MAC) as a context-sensitive spatial accessibility measure using the national average facility-to-population ratio as a benchmark and explore how fixed thresholds can over- or underestimate accessibility compared with MAC in a nationwide U.S. analysis. Using the national benchmark, MAC measures the minimum travel time required to reach the national average level of a given resource in each zone, accounting for the geographic distributions of demand and resources. By comparing MAC with multiple fixed thresholds (i.e., 30, 60, 90, and 120 minutes), we find that MAC is sensitive to geographic contexts in terms of the distributions of demand and resources. This approach enables direct geographic comparisons of spatial accessibility to different resources and provides evidence to support effective policy interventions by providing more context-sensitive accessibility estimates.

articles.title: Representation of Police in Television, 2020 Anti-Police Movements, and Audience Reception
articles.abstract: Police television is one of the most popular genres of television in the modern age. With its continued popularity and high viewership, police television, from fictional to reality shows, is often the first introduction to the criminal justice system for many viewers. Prior research has also shown that many people believe that the information they see on police television is factual and reflective of reality, whether this information is fact checked or not. In fact, the police institution relies on its cultural power to sustain its status as maintainers of social order and of regulators of deviance. However, with the 2020 anti-police brutality movements, the public atmosphere around police undeniably shifted toward a more negative outlook than before. With this question, I seek to identify whether or not there has been a change in the way police officers are portrayed in television, and if so, how change has been implemented. In addition, I seek to find how police television continues to curate a specific image of police officers without ignoring the social movements that were present. Through the qualitative observation of two television shows, I explore the changes in portrayals of police officers across the two shows. I find that there are more varied portrayals of police officers in specific categories, yet police officers are still shown to be the sole method of maintaining social order and controlling deviance. The police television shows observed in this paper adhere to the promotion of “ideal cop” principles to show the effectiveness of police officers in regulating society.

articles.title: The Qualitative Network Approach: A Methodological Framework and Tutorial for Relational Coding
articles.authors: Ivonne Lipsch-Wijnen, Femke Nijland, Vanessa Torres van Grinsven, Szilvia Zörgő, Gjalt-Jorn Peters
articles.abstract: Relationships between concepts are often interpreted during qualitative analysis but may remain implicit within coding structures, thematic descriptions, or analytical narratives. This article introduces the Qualitative Network Approach (QNA), a methodological framework for representing qualitative codes as interconnected elements. Its associated method, QNA network coding, specifies interpreted connections between pairs of qualitative codes according to relationship type and, where relevant, directionality. A four-step tutorial demonstrates how researchers can identify two concepts in the data for relational interpretation, identify and specify their relationship using the codebook, assign the three codes to the data fragment, and document a QNA network code. A worked interview example illustrates how individual QNA network codes can form a wider QNA network code structure. QNA may be useful when relationships between concepts are analytically important. By making relational interpretations explicit and traceable to the underlying data, QNA aims to increase the transparency and inspectability of qualitative analysis.

articles.title: Sentiment change points, not peaks, mark when public opinion has yet to settle
articles.authors: Chenying Weng, Yilun Chen, Huazhen Huang, Yiting Yang, He Gong, Hongkai Wang
articles.abstract: Timing interventions during public controversies requires more than identifying when sentiment is strongest: a peak does not tell us whether public opinion can still change. We analyzed about 1.34M Weibo posts about a controversial news event (Company T vs. Company L), separating sentiment strength by referent and tracking the resulting trajectories across the event. After sudden change points (SCPs) sentiment-strength trajectories and public expression continued to change; after peak points (PPs) they largely stabilized (mean absolute displacement 3.291 times; p = 0.035), and discourse-strategy composition changed around SCPs but stayed largely stable around PPs. SCPs, not PPs, are the candidate leverage points. This suggests that the strongest moment is where public opinion settles, so mitigation should act at the SCP.

articles.title: Integrating Green Marketing and Environmental Behavior to Predict Revisit Intention in Indonesian Ecotourism
articles.authors: Andina Fasha, Cheryn Kang, Lady Lady, Budi Setiawan
articles.abstract: Purpose: The escalation of ecotourism as sustainability-oriented travel highlights the inconsistency of tourists' responsible actions during visits, which is also known as the attitude-behavior gap, whereas environmental concern does not necessarily translate into action, as discussed in sustainable tourism literature. Research Methodology: A quantitative approach was employed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling, collected through questionnaire surveys from 478 tourists who had previously visited Ecotourism destinations in Batam City, Indonesia, using SmartPLS 4. Results: The findings show how direct environmental experiences at the destination were more effective in encouraging responsible tourist behavior than pre-visit digital exposure, which presumes that it is more likely to develop revisit intentions as long-term destination loyalty. Conclusions: The study highlights the importance of environmental behavior in fostering revisit intention within ecotourism destinations and suggests that direct interpretive experiences at the destination may play a more influential role in shaping tourists’ behavior than digital promotional exposure alone. Limitations: This study was limited to one ecotourism site in Batam City, with cross-sectional self-reported data, which may have limited generalizability. Contributions: This study extends sustainable tourism literature by integrating digital green marketing, environmental belief, and environmental interpretation into a unified behavioral framework explaining revisit intention through environmental behavior and offer practical insights for ecotourism managers to strengthen sustainable behavior and long-term destination loyalty through effective communication and interpretation strategies.

articles.title: The nirvana fallacy and the case for friction in responding to online child sexual abuse

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: On 3 April 2026 the European Union’s temporary exception for voluntary detection of child sexual abuse material lapsed, and for three months the alternative that perfectionist arguments rarely state became policy: to do nothing. During the previous gap, in 2020–21, reports of abuse material from the EU fell by 58%. This article names the reasoning behind such outcomes as the nirvana fallacy, which Demsetz identified in 1969 as measuring the imperfect against an ideal instead of the real alternative. Four forms recur in the child-safety debate: circumvention, false positives, categorical impossibility and the slippery slope. Each states a real issue and leaves its comparator unstated. The article reframes the measures as friction, drawing on situational crime prevention, public health harm reduction and the economics of adversarial systems, then works along the offending pathway to set out what each friction layer achieves and what it cannot. Randomised trials and field deployments on Google Search, Pornhub and the Tor search engine Ahmia.fi show warnings reducing attempted access and increasing help-seeking, while hash matching, classifiers and age assurance carry known limits alongside measured effects. The article does not propose weakening encryption, and argues that most serious objections to other controls should be treated as design constraints rather than as refusals. A comparative test of four questions applies to objections and proposals alike, along with eight recommendations. Layered friction reduces measured offending-related behaviour at nearly every point it has been tested, and children are safer with it in the system than without it.

articles.title: Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis: A Methodological Architecture for Human–AI Collaboration in Qualitative Inquiry
articles.abstract: When generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is adopted without attention to its epistemological implications, postpositivist commitments to truth-seeking over meaning-making risk becoming more entrenched in qualitative inquiry, eroding reflexivity and interpretive depth. This has prompted scholars to call for the GenAI debate to move beyond binary adoption-or-refusal framings, toward how GenAI might be deployed while preserving reflexivity, theoretical depth, and epistemological plurality. I outline Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis (LICA), an interpretivist human–AI collaboration architecture, as a methodological answer to this call. LICA operationalises the position of Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism. It maintains distinct human and computational interpretive layers across six analytic steps. The architecture is centred on the live interpretation interview, which yields an initial participant narrative and a co-constructed interpretive narration negotiated between the participant and researcher. The initial narrative serves as a basis for thematic analysis, while the co-constructed interpretive narration grounds ideal-type analysis. Findings are brought together into a thematic-typological integrative analysis, which addresses what the complete thematic-typological configuration means in relation to the research question, and clarifies what it reveals about the underlying reflexive processes and human–AI collaboration. Throughout the process, human–AI divergences are retained and warranted as potential sources of analytic insights, while a traceable genealogy links successive analytic constructs to their empirical origins and interpretative context. Rather than accelerating an existing workflow, LICA relocates analytic effort to the research encounter and structures computational participation to interrogate interpretive judgement and reflexivity. For contexts where GenAI use raises strong ethical, environmental, or participant-vulnerability concerns, the method can be adapted into Layered Interpretive Analysis (LIA), a non-computational variant which retains key features of explicit meaning co-construction and thematic-typological integration.
